options.text: Earth’s largest waterfall is underwater between Greenland and Iceland. Cold Nordic water sinks beneath warmer water and spills down a drop in the seabed.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: In 1941, HMS Hood sank here during a 16-minute battle with the Bismarck. Only three of the 1,415 people aboard survived.
options.label: Royal Navy

options.text: Instruments between Greenland and Iceland have measured pulses of deep water sweeping through roughly every five days. Even the current at the bottom of this strait has a rhythm.
options.label: Journal of Physical Oceanography

options.text: Sea ice can drift south through the Denmark Strait from the Arctic. It hugs the Greenland side as the East Greenland Current carries it past Iceland.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The vaquita lives only in the northern Gulf of California. No other whale, dolphin, or porpoise has such a small range.
options.label: NOAA Fisheries

options.text: More than 3½ km beneath the gulf, a research robot filmed what looks like an upside-down waterfall. Hot vent fluid rises and spills around a rock overhang.
options.label: MBARI expedition footage

options.text: Some islands here were once joined to the mainland by land bridges. On others, wildlife had to arrive by sea or air.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Gulf of California is opening along a plate boundary. Baja California rides with the Pacific Plate while most of mainland Mexico stays on the North American Plate.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: There is a pool with its own surface beneath the sea at East Flower Garden Bank. Water seeping out of a salt dome is so salty and dense that it settles into a hollow under ordinary seawater.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Some coral reefs in the northwestern gulf sit on hills pushed up by salt. Deep deposits rose under the seabed, lifting the tops of the banks into sunlit water.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Rings of warm Caribbean water can break away from the Loop Current. They travel west across the gulf long after the main current has turned towards Florida.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Water can enter the gulf from the Caribbean, swing far north and leave again beside Florida. This Loop Current feeds the Gulf Stream before it heads across the Atlantic.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: A Greek trading ship survived intact more than two kilometres beneath the Black Sea. The deep water lacks oxygen, allowing even ancient wood to survive.
options.label: University of Southampton

options.text: The sea has a second, ancient coastline. Researchers have mapped prehistoric shorelines about 150 metres beneath today’s surface.
options.label: University of Rhode Island

options.text: The Black Sea can look turquoise from space. Blooms of microscopic plankton covered in chalky plates can turn the surface milky blue.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Black Sea trades water with the Mediterranean in two directions through one strait. Fresher Black Sea water flows out near the surface of the Bosporus while saltier water flows in underneath.
options.label: whoi.edu

options.text: The Aral Sea once acted like a giant radiator for the surrounding land. As it shrank, nearby winters grew colder and summers grew hotter and drier.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: As the water grew too salty for familiar catches, fisheries turned to an introduced flatfish. Flounder could survive where many of the old commercial species could no longer live.
options.label: documents.worldbank.org

options.text: The Aral Sea's shoreline retreated in part because cotton was being grown far upstream. Water diverted to irrigate fields never finished the journey to the lake.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In 2014 the entire eastern lobe of the South Aral Sea dried up. Within a human lifetime, a basin that helped make this the fourth-largest lake on Earth had become land.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Vjetrenica Cave breathes with the seasons. Stand at its mouth in warm weather and air blows out toward you. In cold weather it flows the other way.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Look closely at the region’s medieval gravestones, called stećci, and you can find people dancing, hunting, and jousting.
options.label: UNESCO nomination evaluation

options.text: A medieval Jewish manuscript survived World War II in Bosnia. Sarajevo’s National Museum recounts that it was sheltered in a mosque in a mountain village, then returned to the museum.
options.label: National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina

options.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches the Adriatic through a narrow strip at Neum. Until Croatia bridged the bay in 2022, the main coastal drive to Dubrovnik crossed Bosnia twice.
options.label: regions-and-cities.ec.europa.eu

options.text: Serbia has inland sand dunes. Wind piled up the Deliblato Sands in the Pannonian plain, hundreds of kilometres from a beach.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Danube has moved since land parcels along the Serbia–Croatia border were surveyed. Following the present river and following the old parcel lines gives two different answers about which country owns some riverbank land.
options.label: europarl.europa.eu

options.text: A river in eastern Serbia runs through three enormous natural stone gates in one gorge. At Vratna, parts of an old cave roof survive as bridges over the water.
options.label: geoparkdjerdap.rs

options.text: Some sand in Namibia’s coastal dunes travelled thousands of kilometres to get there, carried first by a river, then by ocean currents, and finally by wind.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fog is the main source of water for life in the Namib Sand Sea. That bank of fog rolling in from the Atlantic helps sustain animals in the dunes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Follow the narrow finger in Namibia’s northeast and you reach the Zambezi. An 1890 agreement between Britain and Germany drew that corridor to give the colony access to the river.
options.label: International Boundary Study

options.text: Namibia's Fish River can shrink to a trickle in the dry season. Over geological time it has carved a canyon as much as 550 metres deep into the southern plateau.
options.label: mme.gov.na

options.text: Some of the black bitumen used to embalm Egyptian mummies came from the Dead Sea. Researchers have traced the material in mummy samples back to its source.
options.label: Archaeometry

options.text: The Jordan River flows into the Dead Sea, but no river flows out. Water escapes by evaporation, leaving salts behind.
options.label: ESA

options.text: The neat rectangles visible from space at the southern end of the Dead Sea are evaporation ponds for harvesting minerals.
options.label: ESA

options.text: The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest exposed land on Earth. You can stand more than 400 metres below ocean level with open sky above you.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Some Danube water reaches the North Sea. In southern Germany it sinks into limestone, resurfaces in a spring, and joins the Rhine. The main Danube continues east to the Black Sea.
options.label: Swabian Alb Geopark

options.text: Float downstream and the Danube takes you past four national capitals in order: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
options.label: International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River

options.text: Where the Danube meets the Black Sea, people have used the delta’s reeds to build their houses and fences.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Danube's drainage basin reaches into 19 countries, more than any other international river basin. A raindrop can start in a country the Danube never visits and still end up in the river.
options.label: icpdr.org

options.text: A magnitude-5.7 earthquake beneath Lake Taupō in 2022 sent two small tsunamis across this inland lake.
options.label: GNS Science

options.text: At Mine Bay, a 14-metre face looks out over the lake. Matahi Brightwell led the carving of his ancestor Ngātoroirangi into a cliff reached by water; the work took four years.
options.label: Destination Great Lake Taupō

options.text: Ngāti Tūwharetoa fishers lowered bundles of bracken fern to the lakebed. Freshwater crayfish sheltered among the fronds, and the fishers lifted the bundles into their canoes.
options.label: Earth Sciences New Zealand

options.text: New Zealand's largest lake fills the caldera of a volcano. The Waikato River, the country's longest, flows out of Lake Taupō on its way to the Tasman Sea.
options.label: doc.govt.nz

options.text: In one Māori account, the South Island is Māui’s canoe. The North Island is the fish he hauled up with a hook fashioned from his ancestor’s jawbone.
options.label: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

options.text: A male kākāpō digs a shallow bowl, settles into it at night, and booms for a mate. The hollow helps his calls resonate.
options.label: Department of Conservation

options.text: A newly hatched tuatara has a light-sensitive third eye on top of its head. Skin grows over it as the animal matures.
options.label: Department of Conservation

options.text: The plates beneath New Zealand swap roles. The Pacific Plate dives beneath the North Island, while near the south of the South Island the Australian Plate goes underneath the Pacific Plate.
options.label: gns.cri.nz

options.text: Baikal has its own landlocked seal. Some seals follow the Angara River out of the lake, but their home waters are deep inside Siberia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal’s golomyanka gives birth to live young. The tail of the small species is so transparent that print can be read through it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal holds roughly a fifth of the world’s unfrozen surface freshwater. Its basin has been collecting water for some 25 million years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal is the world's deepest lake. Its water surface is above sea level, but its deepest floor lies more than a kilometre below the level of the ocean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The long ridges rising out of Lake Superior on Isle Royale began as lava flows over a billion years ago. Much later, an ice sheet scoured them into sharper relief.
options.label: NASA

options.text: From orbit, winter clouds over Lake Superior can look like streets. Cold air crossing the open water picks up moisture that falls as snow on the far shore.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Around 1900 there were no moose on Isle Royale. Biologists think the first arrivals swam across from the mainland.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Lake Superior alone holds more water than the other four Great Lakes combined. Its nearly 12,100 cubic kilometres slightly outweigh Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario put together.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Between Florida and the Bahamas, oceanographers measure a current with a submarine cable. Salt water moving through Earth's magnetic field creates a voltage that changes with the flow.
options.label: aoml.noaa.gov

options.text: Bermuda lies in a sea whose boundaries are currents. The Sargasso Sea shifts with the circulation of the North Atlantic, so its limits cannot be drawn by following a coastline.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: The Triangle's northern corner is the top of a submerged volcanic mountain. The pale limestone islands of Bermuda sit on a much older volcanic foundation.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The world's shortest scheduled passenger flight connects two of the UK's Orkney Islands. Westray and Papa Westray are close enough for the flight to take about two minutes.
options.label: loganair.co.uk

options.text: Water can travel upstream on the River Severn as a moving wall. A large incoming tide is squeezed into the narrowing estuary quickly enough to produce a wave that surfers can ride inland.
options.label: severnestuarypartnership.org.uk

options.text: Stand on the historic prime meridian at Greenwich and a GPS receiver will put you west of zero longitude. The modern zero line passes about 102 metres east of the brass strip.
options.label: rmg.co.uk

options.text: In the Chaîne des Puys, a line of volcanoes sits next to a great fault. Together they record an early stage of a continent pulling apart, right in the middle of France.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Burgundy a climat can be a particular plot of vines. Centuries of growers divided slopes by differences in soil, aspect and the wine each patch produced.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Roman aqueduct supplying Nîmes had to cross the Gardon valley. Its builders stacked three tiers of arches at the Pont du Gard to keep water high enough to flow onward by gravity.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: France's longest land border is with Brazil. It runs along the edge of French Guiana, an ocean away from Paris.
options.label: gov.br

options.text: In the western Caucasus, explorers descended more than two kilometres below the entrance of Krubera Cave. A second cave in the same region, Veryovkina, also passes the two-kilometre mark.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tbilisi’s name points to something you can still feel there. The Georgian word for “warm” refers to the city’s sulfur springs.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The anthem adopted after Georgia’s Rose Revolution borrowed its music from two operas, Abesalom da Eteri and Daisi.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Georgia has rainforests on the Black Sea. In the Colchic lowlands, extraordinary rainfall sustains peat bogs in a warm temperate forest landscape.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Several of Germany’s great rivers carry water north. The exception begins in the Black Forest: the Danube sets off east across Europe.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: One possible origin for Berlin’s name is a Slavic word for swamp, a clue to the landscape along the Spree where the settlement grew.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The tune used for Germany’s national anthem began as an Austrian imperial anthem composed by Joseph Haydn.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The seabed off Germany's North Sea coast is part of the world's largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats. At low tide, the Wadden Sea turns into land you can walk on.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Greece sings only two stanzas of a much longer poem. The original Hymn to Liberty, inspired by the 1821 uprising, has 158.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The country’s Greek name, Elláda, and the English name Greece come by different routes. English inherited the Roman name Graecia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Trace Greece beyond its peninsulas and the outline breaks into an archipelago. The Factbook counts roughly 2,000 islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Peloponnese is called a peninsula, but today you can sail all the way around it. The Corinth Canal cuts straight through its narrow land connection to the rest of Greece.
options.label: corinthcanal.com

options.text: Greenland’s ice sheet holds nearly seven percent of the world’s freshwater. Only Antarctica has a larger ice sheet.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Kalaallit Nunaat, the Greenlandic name for Greenland, means “land of the people.” The Norse name is traditionally credited to Erik the Red trying to attract settlers.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Greenland’s capital changed names in 1979. The Danish Godthåb meant “good hope,” while the Greenlandic Nuuk describes a cape.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Ilulissat, icebergs can run aground on a submerged sill at the mouth of the fjord. They may have to melt or break apart before they can reach the open sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Danube once separated cities whose names you can still see on a map of Budapest. Buda stood on the west bank and Pest on the east before unification in 1873.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Danube and Tisza divide Hungary into three broad stretches of country. One Hungarian name to look for on a river map is Duna, the Danube.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Hungarians call their country Magyarország, the country of the Magyars. The English name Hungary came through a different name used for peoples arriving on the eastern European steppes.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Central Europe's largest lake is shallow enough to average only about three metres deep. Hungary's Lake Balaton stretches almost 80 kilometres from end to end.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: Listen to a Tosk choir in southern Albania and you can hear a single “e” held beneath two solo voices. The singers take turns breathing, so the note never breaks.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Outside Tirana, a bunker runs five storeys underground and contains 106 rooms. Visitors can now walk through it as a museum of Albania’s dictatorship.
options.label: Bunk’Art

options.text: In Albania’s northern highlands, a traditional garment called the xhubleta flares out in rippling folds like a bell. Its distinctive silhouette is built by hand from felt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Vjosa crosses from Greece into Albania and runs freely to the Adriatic. In 2023 Albania made its stretch and several tributaries Europe's first wild river national park.
options.label: iucn.org

options.text: In Andorra’s national anthem the country itself speaks. Its history is sung in the first person.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The capital’s Catalan name, Andorra la Vella, means “Andorra the Old.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Andorra survives from a belt of frontier states that Charlemagne established in the Pyrenees. Its position between France and Spain goes back to that frontier.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: A single glacial valley system takes up almost a tenth of Andorra. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror landscape alone covers more than 4,000 hectares.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Near Baku, a line of flames burns along the foot of a hillside called Yanardag. The fuel seeps straight from the ground as natural gas.

options.text: On Gobustan’s dry hills, ancient artists carved boats and fish into the rock. One explanation is that the Caspian stood much higher then, almost turning the hills into islands.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Sheki and Basgal, makers of silk kelaghayi scarves print their designs with wooden stamps. A mixture containing resin and wax protects parts of the silk when the cloth is dyed.

options.text: Azerbaijan borders Turkey, but you cannot reach that border from Baku without leaving the country. The entire Turkish frontier belongs to the detached territory of Nakhchivan.

options.text: Landlocked Belarus sheds water towards two different seas. A little over half its surface runoff goes towards the Black Sea, while the rest goes towards the Baltic.
options.label: oecd.org

options.text: One Belarusian bog contains over a hundred lakes. At Yelnia they sit among raised peatlands that rise above the surrounding low country.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: The Pripyat in Belarus can turn fields and woods into an inland sea each spring. Along its middle course the river still has room to spread kilometres across its natural floodplain.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: One tradition places the writing of Belgium’s anthem in a Brussels café during the 1830 revolution. Among the writers was an actor from the theatre associated with the uprising.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Belgium’s name recalls the Belgae, peoples whose territory stretched between the English Channel and the Rhine in antiquity.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The name Brussels preserves an older landscape: its Germanic roots refer to a dwelling and a marsh.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: In Baarle, pockets of Belgium contain pockets of the Netherlands. The border winds through streets and even houses, where the front door can determine the address.
options.label: m-en.visitbaarle.com

options.text: The song that became Bulgaria’s anthem was composed in 1885 by a student on his way to fight in the war with Serbia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bulgaria’s capital takes its name from a church. Parts of the Church of Saint Sofia may date as far back as the fourth century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bulgaria took its name from the Bulgars, a people of Central Asian origin who joined local Slavic inhabitants to form a state in the late seventh century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The highest point anywhere on the Balkan Peninsula is in Bulgaria. Musala in the Rila Mountains rises to 2,925 metres, a little higher than Mount Olympus in Greece.

options.text: Off Croatia’s Adriatic coast, an atlas has to account for roughly 1,200 islands, islets, rocks and ridges. Most of the Adriatic’s islands lie on this side.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The words of Croatia’s anthem were written in 1835. The song was adopted officially in 1972, while Croatia was still part of Yugoslavia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: An old explanation of Zagreb’s name puts the settlement “beyond the ditch.” The two parts of the name describe where to find it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: You can now drive from the rest of Croatia to Dubrovnik without a border crossing. The Pelješac Bridge bypasses the strip of Bosnian coast that splits Croatia's mainland shoreline.
options.label: regions-and-cities.ec.europa.eu

options.text: In the Moravian Karst, a boat can pass through caves on the underground Punkva River. Partway through the route, the cave opens to daylight at the bottom of the Macocha Abyss.
options.label: visitczechia.com

options.text: Europe’s largest natural sandstone arch stands in a piece of Czechia called Bohemian Switzerland. The arch is what erosion left of a much larger mass of sandstone.
options.label: visitczechia.com

options.text: At Český Krumlov the Vltava doubles back around the old town. The bends of the river still trace the shape of the medieval settlement beneath its castle.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Danish mainland is only part of the country’s outline. More than 400 islands lie in the Danish archipelago.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Copenhagen’s name describes its old trade: its Danish roots mean a merchants’ harbour.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Denmark has two anthems of equal standing. A royal anthem dating to 1780 is used on occasions attended by royalty.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Kingdom of Denmark acquired a land border with Canada in 2022. It crosses a tiny Arctic island called Tartupaluk, or Hans Island, between Greenland and Ellesmere Island.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: Estonia and Finland sing different words to the same anthem melody. In Estonia the song was banned during Soviet rule.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tallinn’s name has been traced to an Estonian expression for “Danish fort,” a reminder of the Danes who established a stronghold there in 1219.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Estonia’s low mainland gives way to an archipelago of more than 1,500 islands in the Baltic.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Kaali on the island of Saaremaa, what looks like a little round woodland pond occupies the largest of a group of meteorite impact craters.
options.label: visitestonia.com

options.text: The Faroe Islands carry sheep in their name: the Old Norse words behind it mean “sheep islands.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tórshavn, the Faroese capital, is named for Thor. Its name means “Thor’s harbour.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: People lived in the Faroes by about AD 500, centuries before the ninth-century Viking settlers arrived. The identity of those earlier islanders is uncertain.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Nowhere in the Faroe Islands is more than about five kilometres from the sea. Even the middle of the largest island is close to a fjord or an Atlantic shore.
options.label: visitfaroeislands.com

options.text: A desert lake can be a nursery. Nile crocodiles breed on Turkana’s islands, while submerged beds of pondweed shelter spawning fish in South Island’s muddy bays.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Koobi Fora, the ground beside the lake preserves early human relatives alongside molluscs and other animals. Researchers use the shells as well as the bones to reconstruct the landscape those humans inhabited.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On a map of bird migration, this arid part of Kenya is a water stop. Migrating waterbirds use the national parks around the world’s largest desert lake.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Turkana is the world's largest permanent desert lake. A great expanse of water survives in this arid basin because rivers bring in rain that fell elsewhere.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Eight locks on the Saimaa Canal make a staircase from Finland's lake district down to the Gulf of Finland. A lake vessel can reach the Baltic without following Saimaa's natural outlet.
options.label: visitlappeenranta.fi

options.text: In the Saimaa Geopark a glacier left a boulder balanced on a tiny patch of bedrock. The Finnish name Kummakivi means “strange stone”.
options.label: saimaageopark.fi

options.text: The water leaving Saimaa at Imatra once thundered through a narrow rock gorge. Hydropower diverted the flow, so seeing the rapids run today depends on a release of water.
options.label: saimaageopark.fi

options.text: A Lake Eyre dragon can make a living on the dry lakebed. This little lizard hunts ants and slips beneath the salt crust for shelter.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: The flood that revives Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre can begin far outside South Australia. Monsoon rains in Queensland feed channels that carry the water across the arid interior.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: As floodwater evaporates and turns to brine, most fish disappear. The Lake Eyre hardyhead can keep feeding and breeding in water saltier than the sea.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: Australia's lowest natural point is a lakebed you can often see. The floor of Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre lies roughly 15 metres below sea level and is usually exposed.
options.label: ga.gov.au

options.text: At Brochet on Reindeer Lake's northern shore, the road connection is seasonal. When the winter road closes, aircraft provide the transport link that trucks do in winter.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: Reindeer Lake receives water from a lake with two exits. Rain falling on upstream Wollaston Lake can travel towards Hudson Bay through Reindeer Lake or take a different outlet towards the Arctic Ocean.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Water levels on this huge northern lake changed when a dam was built at Whitesand Rapids in the 1940s. Reindeer Lake was used to store water for a hydroelectric station farther down the river system.
options.label: gladue.drc.usask.ca

options.text: The Slave River is building land inside Great Slave Lake. At its mouth, sediment spreads into branching channels and wetlands that researchers have watched shift in successive satellite images.
options.label: ntrs.nasa.gov

options.text: Great Slave Lake has two strikingly different underwater landscapes. The river-fed western basin is relatively shallow and cloudy, while the eastern arm contains clear, exceptionally deep water.
options.label: publications.gc.ca

options.text: Great Slave Lake has a fish called inconnu, French for “unknown”. Some populations leave the lake to spawn in tributaries, linking the lake fishery to rivers well inland.
options.label: publications.gc.ca

options.text: On the west shore of Lake Winnipegosis, seaside plantain grows far inland. Salty flats give plants usually found on northern coasts a foothold in the boreal forest.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: Springs beside this freshwater lake discharge brine. Its chemistry records groundwater dissolving rock salt and mixing with fresh water on the way up.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: You can walk from boreal vegetation into salt-tolerant meadow plants on the same lakeshore. As sheets of lakebed emerge, their poorly drained, salty soil sorts out what can grow there.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: Lake Winnipegosis is upstream of two much larger names on the map. Its water goes by the Waterhen River into Lake Manitoba, then onward into Lake Winnipeg.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: The Narrows separate a small, shallow southern basin from a much larger northern one. The southern basin averages only about nine metres deep.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: Winnipeg sits south of its namesake lake. The Red River carries water north from the city into the lake, away from the US border.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: The lake drains into Hudson Bay by the Nelson River. Water from the Canadian prairie thus rounds off its journey on the shore of a subarctic sea.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: Lake Winnipeg collects runoff from an area roughly forty times its own surface. A relatively shallow lake is the outlet for a basin reaching from the Rockies into the United States.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: On Onega's eastern shore, people pecked birds and other figures directly into the rock. The carvings form a World Heritage site with another group about 300 kilometres away on the White Sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Onega straddles a geological seam. Its basin sits partly on the ancient Baltic Shield and partly on the Russian Platform.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: The surface of this enormous inland lake sits only about 35 metres above the Baltic. Parts of its bed are well below sea level.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: Europe's second-largest lake drains straight towards its largest. Water leaving Lake Onega follows the Svir into Lake Ladoga before reaching the Baltic.

options.text: Off the Lofoten Islands lies the Røst Reef, an immense coral reef growing in deep, cold water beyond the reach of sunlight.
options.label: Source

options.text: About 8,000 years ago part of the seabed off Norway slid downhill. The tsunami it sent across the sea left layers of sand on the Scottish coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: Herring spend the feeding season where Arctic and Atlantic waters meet. When the shoals head for their Norwegian wintering grounds, killer whales follow them.
options.label: Source

options.text: Water heading into the Arctic from the Atlantic crosses the Norwegian Sea. Its warm northward route carries ocean heat past the Arctic Circle along Norway.
options.label: awi.de

options.text: In parts of the Celtic Sea, fishery scientists count burrows with underwater cameras. The holes in the muddy bottom give away Norway lobsters that spend much of the day hidden.
options.label: oar.marine.ie

options.text: Off Pembrokeshire, Grassholm looks white from a distance in the breeding season. Its crowded colony of northern gannets turns a small Celtic Sea island into a conspicuous landmark.
options.label: rspb.org.uk

options.text: A front in the Celtic Sea can separate communities of jelly-like animals. On one side the tide mixes the water column, while on the other it leaves a warmer layer floating on top.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: Sonar revealed enormous hollows beneath the Strait of Dover. Researchers traced them to waterfalls spilling from an ice-dammed lake when a land bridge still joined Britain and France.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Channel Tunnel is actually three tunnels. A service tunnel runs between the two railway tunnels, with cross-passages every 375 metres.
options.label: Source

options.text: The first recorded unaided swim across the Channel took 21 hours and 45 minutes. Matthew Webb made it from England to France in 1875.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel, the English Channel has tides large enough to redraw the coastline in hours. Water sweeps across sandbanks around an abbey perched above them on a rock.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The tallest sand dune in Europe is moving inland from the Bay of Biscay. At the Dune du Pilat, wind carries sand over the crest and slowly buries the forest behind it.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: A milky patch in the Bay of Biscay can be a bloom of microscopic plankton. The chalk plates they make around their cells reflect sunlight back through the water.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: European anchovies spawn in the Bay of Biscay in spring. The fishery here depends on where currents carry eggs and larvae long before the young fish join a school.
options.label: academic.oup.com

options.text: More than five kilometres of water lie off the coast of Greece. The Calypso Deep, in the Hellenic Trench, is the Mediterranean's deepest known point.
options.label: journals.ametsoc.org

options.text: Sailors nicknamed Stromboli the lighthouse of the Mediterranean. Frequent bursts of incandescent lava could be seen at night from ships passing the volcanic island.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Mediterranean has a buried floor of salt. Around six million years ago its connection to the Atlantic narrowed so much that evaporation left thick salt deposits beneath what is now deep sea.
options.label: nature.com

options.text: Woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island for thousands of years after they disappeared from most of the mainland. Some were still alive around 4,000 years ago.
options.label: Source

options.text: Open water can persist beside Wrangel Island even when ice covers the sea around it. These recurring openings are called polynyas.
options.label: Source

options.text: Pacific eiders nest on tundra around this sea, including Wrangel Island. After breeding, they travel through the Chukchi Sea to spend winter in the Bering Sea.
options.label: Source

options.text: Between the New Siberian Islands and Wrangel Island, the Arctic Ocean spreads across a broad, shallow shelf. The East Siberian Sea covers land that was exposed during lower ice-age seas.
options.label: pame.is

options.text: Rock worn off the Himalayas ends up far out beneath the bay. Rivers deliver it to the Bengal Fan, a submarine pile of sediment stretching about 3,000 kilometres.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the northern bay, rain and river water can leave a layer of fresher water only about 15 metres deep floating on the saltier sea.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the Sundarbans at the head of the bay, tigers swim long distances between mangrove islands. Fish and crabs are among the prey they take in this tidal forest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A layer of relatively fresh water floats on the Bay of Bengal. Monsoon rain and river discharge make its surface markedly fresher than that of the Arabian Sea on the other side of India.
options.label: drs.nio.res.in

options.text: The Yamato Rise is a broad underwater highland in the middle of the Sea of Japan. It separates deep basins in much the way a mountain range divides lowlands on land.
options.label: emecs.or.jp

options.text: In cold winters, surface water can become dense enough to sink and renew deep water within the Sea of Japan. The basin makes much of its own deep water behind its shallow entrances.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: The Tsushima Warm Current brings heat north past the Japanese islands. Some of this water eventually escapes through the Tsugaru Strait into the Pacific.
options.label: emecs.or.jp

options.text: On their migration along the Asian coast, spoon-billed sandpipers stop to feed on the Yellow Sea mudflats. Look closely at one and even the tip of its tiny bill flares out like a spoon.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In satellite pictures, turquoise and tan swirls can run across this shallow sea. Tides and waves stir fine sediment off the seabed and suspend it in the water.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Korean tidal flats, or getbol, are home to mud octopuses, fiddler crabs and ghost crabs. At low tide a whole stretch of their seafloor becomes dry enough to walk across.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Yellow Sea takes its colour and its name from sediment. Rivers carry such fine mineral grains into this shallow sea that tides can keep them suspended long after they reach salt water.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: The East Australian Current sheds rings of tropical water into the Tasman Sea. A warm patch can travel south inside a rotating eddy after it has detached from the current.
options.label: dcceew.gov.au

options.text: A Tasman Sea marine heatwave lasted more than eight months in 2015–16. An unusually strong southward flow brought warm water to the east coast of Tasmania.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: Ball's Pyramid rises like a blade out of the Tasman Sea near Lord Howe Island. This narrow rock spire is a remnant of an eroded volcano.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In 2019 a crew paddled a dugout canoe from Taiwan to Yonaguni to test how early voyagers might have crossed. It took just over 45 hours, with the island below the horizon for most of the trip.
options.label: National Museum of Nature and Science, Japan

options.text: Off Jeju, haenyeo divers gather abalone and sea urchins on a single breath. When they surface, you can hear the distinctive sound they make as they take in air for the next dive.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Where the Yangtze empties into the East China Sea, divers found a wooden Qing-era merchant vessel. In the murky estuary, one of the few photographs they could take showed porcelain still sitting in rows.
options.label: Shanghai Municipal Government

options.text: In summer, freshwater from China's Yangtze can travel across the East China Sea towards Korea's Jeju Island. Its low-salinity surface plume crosses national waters.
options.label: frontiersin.org

options.text: The North Sea tide rotates around points where the tidal rise and fall is very small. Two ports on opposite sides of such a point can have high water at very different times.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Since 1996, carbon dioxide separated at the Sleipner gas field has been injected into porous sandstone beneath the North Sea. The storage space is in the pores between grains of sand.
options.label: sodir.no

options.text: In 1953, wind drove North Sea water into the narrowing southern basin during a high tide. The same storm flooded coasts in both England and the Netherlands.
options.label: eprints.soton.ac.uk

options.text: At the head of Penzhina Bay, the water can rise and fall by nearly fourteen metres. Some of the Pacific's largest tides occur at this remote end of the Sea of Okhotsk.
options.label: doi.org

options.text: Iron from the Sea of Okhotsk travels into the North Pacific below the surface. This trace nutrient can help feed plankton far from the continental shelf that supplied it.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Sea ice leaves salt behind as it forms. On the northern shelf of the Sea of Okhotsk, the resulting dense water sinks and helps ventilate the North Pacific below its surface.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: A mud volcano off Azerbaijan built an island in early 2023. Satellites watched the Caspian reclaim it almost entirely by the end of 2024.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Caspian has its own species of seal. In winter the seals gather on ice in the shallow north of this landlocked lake to give birth and nurse their pups.
options.label: Source

options.text: On the eastern shore, a narrow channel feeds a salty lagoon called Garabogazköl. A dam closed the channel in 1980 and the lagoon nearly dried up. In 1992 the dam came down.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The world's largest lake ends below the level of the world ocean. Rivers pour into the Caspian, but there is no natural river carrying its water out to sea.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Titicaca water frog wears what looks like a suit several sizes too big. Its folds of skin give it extra surface area to absorb oxygen underwater.
options.label: si.edu

options.text: Lake Titicaca has a river outlet, yet most of the water it loses never enters a river. At this altitude and latitude, evaporation takes away far more water than the Desaguadero carries out.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: Sediment beneath Titicaca records a time when its water level was tens of metres lower. Places now well offshore were once close enough to the surface for shallow-water organisms to live there.
options.label: pubs.geoscienceworld.org

options.text: Tanganyika has a fish that plays the cuckoo’s trick underwater. A cichlid gathering her eggs into her mouth can scoop up catfish eggs too. The catfish hatch first.
options.label: Source

options.text: A passenger ship reached this landlocked lake in crates. A German shipyard built the Graf Goetzen, took it apart for transport, and sent the pieces to be reassembled on Tanganyika.
options.label: Source

options.text: Some freshwater snails here grow such ornate shells that biologists call them “sea-like.” Tanganyika has dozens of snail species found nowhere else.
options.label: Source

options.text: Lake Tanganyika stretches for more than 650 kilometres along an African rift. It is the world's longest freshwater lake, yet you are seldom far from one of its two long shores.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: You can cross from nearly fresh water to salty water without leaving the lake. The Ili River freshens the western basin, and a narrow strait limits how much mixes into the east.
options.label: NASA

options.text: At the lake’s southern edge, the Ili River fans into a wetland in the desert. The same protected area shelters goitered gazelles, marbled polecats and white-headed ducks.
options.label: Source

options.text: Balkhash spends winter under ice. A satellite passing over in March 2026 caught strips of turquoise water opening through the white ice cover.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Water from mountains in China arrives in Kazakhstan and ends its journey at Balkhash. The lake has no outlet to the sea, so water that enters it leaves mainly by evaporation.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Arctic Circle cuts through Great Bear Lake. Its northern and southern shores lie on opposite sides of the latitude used to define the Arctic.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Five long arms meet in a central basin. Water leaving by the Great Bear River starts its outward journey from the southwest arm, called Keith Arm.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: In summer, warmer water can build up in the arms while the middle stays cold. A temperature reading from the shore can give a very misleading picture of the lake.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Great Bear Lake is the largest lake entirely within Canada. The Canadian Great Lakes with larger surface areas all have a US shore as well.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: When wind piles water up toward Buffalo, the level can fall at Toledo, at the other end of the lake. The water then sloshes back, a motion called a seiche.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: On Kelleys Island, you can see deep grooves in the bedrock where a glacier once scraped across what is now Lake Erie.
options.label: Source

options.text: Lake Erie helped snow fall on Buffalo while the trees were still in leaf during the “October Surprise.” Cold air crossing the warmer lake picked up the water that fell as heavy snow downwind.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Erie is the shallowest of the five Great Lakes and the quickest to flush. Its water is replaced on average in less than three years, compared with nearly two centuries in Superior.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Lake Ontario's surface sits roughly a hundred metres lower than Lake Erie's. The connecting Niagara River loses much of that height at Niagara Falls.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Ontario averages about 86 metres deep. That average depth alone is greater than the maximum depth of neighbouring Lake Erie.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Lake Ontario is the last of the five Great Lakes on the journey to the Atlantic. Its outlet becomes the St Lawrence River.
options.label: apps.glerl.noaa.gov

options.text: Ontario has the smallest surface area of the five Great Lakes, yet holds more than three times as much water as Erie. The difference is hidden in its deep basin.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Two volcanoes rise out of the lake to make Ometepe. Concepción and Maderas form the two ends of an island linked by a narrow waist.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Off Granada, the lake breaks into a maze of hundreds of small islands. Their origin lies with Mombacho, the volcano looming above the western shore.
options.label: mapanicaragua.com

options.text: Zapatera is both a lake island and part of a national park. The park includes the smaller islands around it, protecting an archipelago inside Nicaragua's largest lake.
options.label: mined.gob.ni

options.text: Central America's largest lake lies much closer to the Pacific than to the Caribbean, yet drains east. Its outlet is the San Juan River, which carries the water to the Caribbean coast.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Along the south shore, sand dunes rise as high as 30 metres. This moving sand supports rare plants, some of which grow nowhere outside the Athabasca dunes.
options.label: Source

options.text: Some channels near Lake Athabasca change direction. When an ice jam or flood raises the Peace River above the lake, water runs back toward the lake through the delta.
options.label: Government of Canada

options.text: Two piles of chimney stones and a cellar pit mark the first Fort Chipewyan. The trading post was built in 1788 on a rocky point across the lake from the present community.
options.label: Source

options.text: At the west end of Lake Athabasca is one of the world's largest inland freshwater deltas. The Peace and Athabasca river systems meet in a shifting landscape of lakes and channels.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The water entering Nettilling Lake has already crossed another large Arctic lake. The Amadjuak River carries it north into Burwash Bay at Nettilling's southern end.
options.label: pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca

options.text: Nettilling has two distinct halves. Low rocky islands break up its shallower eastern side, while a much more open basin spreads to the west.
options.label: paleo.ulaval.ca

options.text: Meltwater from the Penny Ice Cap carries finely ground rock into Nettilling. Sediment settling on the lake floor preserves a downstream record of changes in a distant ice cap.
options.label: paleo.ulaval.ca

options.text: Indiana has a Great Lakes shoreline. Its short arc of Lake Michigan lies between the much longer shores of Illinois and Michigan.
options.label: in.gov

options.text: Lake Michigan holds almost twelve times as much water as Lake Erie. Two lakes that look broadly comparable on a continental map conceal very different depths.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: At the Indiana Dunes, wind carries sand up from a freshwater shore. A beach beside a lake supplies dunes tall enough to climb like hills.
options.label: in.gov

options.text: Michigan is the only one of the five Great Lakes with every shore in a single country. Canada shares all four of the others with the United States.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Counting its islands, Huron has the longest shoreline of the five Great Lakes. Larger Lake Superior has less shore to follow.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: The Bruce Peninsula nearly walls off Georgian Bay from the main lake. Stand on one shore of the peninsula and you face the bay, then cross to the other side and you still face Lake Huron.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Huron's water is partway through a staircase of lakes. It leaves by the St Clair River, crosses Lake St Clair and continues through the Detroit River to Erie.
options.label: apps.glerl.noaa.gov

options.text: Lake Huron contains the world's largest island in a freshwater lake. Manitoulin Island is itself large enough to hold lakes with islands of their own.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: Beausoleil Island has a change of scenery rare enough to fit two landscapes on one trail. Its south has hardwood forest, while its north has exposed Canadian Shield rock and wind-bent pines.
options.label: parks.canada.ca

options.text: At the Grotto on Georgian Bay, waves have hollowed a cave into the limestone of the Bruce Peninsula. Its blue pool connects to the bay through an underwater opening.
options.label: parks.canada.ca

options.text: A wooden schooner lies just below the surface at the edge of Georgian Bay. Researchers put instruments around the Sweepstakes to find out how much passing boats disturb the wreck.
options.label: journals.plos.org

options.text: During the siege of Leningrad, trucks crossed Ladoga on a winter ice road. A pipeline and an electric cable also crossed the lake, laid on its bed.
options.label: Source

options.text: Ladoga has its own freshwater ringed seals. Scientists studying when the seals became isolated found an unexpected second line of evidence in the DNA of the lice living on them.
options.label: Source

options.text: On the Valaam archipelago in Lake Ladoga, a monastery rises above the islands. Even the monks’ outer gate has a church built over it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Ladoga is Europe's largest lake. A relatively short river, the Neva, drains this enormous basin through Saint Petersburg into the Baltic.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: A papyrus delta at Lake Albert is hunting country for the shoebill. The Semliki deposits sediment in shallow water where a bird can stand almost motionless waiting for fish.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Oil reached the surface beside Lake Albert long before drill rigs did. Natural seeps in western Uganda drew early petroleum explorers to the rift valley.
options.label: petroleum.go.ug

options.text: At Kibiro on Lake Albert's shore, people harvest salt from soil. They wash the salt out of the earth and boil down the resulting brine, then reuse the soil in another cycle.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Along the rocky shore live small, brightly coloured cichlids called mbuna. The lake has produced hundreds of related fish species, many found only here.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: What looks like smoke rising from the water can be a swarm of tiny lake flies. On shore the flies are collected and pressed together to make kungu cakes.
options.label: Source

options.text: A drill lowered into Lake Malawi recovered mud recording 1.3 million years of climate. It showed stretches of extreme drought interrupting periods when the basin overflowed.
options.label: Source

options.text: One long rift lake has three names on the map. Malawi calls it Lake Malawi, Mozambique uses Niassa, and on the Tanzanian shore it is Nyasa.
options.label: ramsar.org

options.text: Thunderstorms here often grow over open water after dark. Night breezes blow from the cooling shores toward each other and lift moist air above the lake.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Lake Victoria produced roughly 500 species of cichlid in about 15,000 years. Mixing between two older fish lineages gave their descendants a head start in genetic variety.
options.label: Source

options.text: Around 15,000 years ago, this vast lake dried out. Mud cores from widely separated parts of the basin preserve the evidence of the dry interval.
options.label: Source

options.text: Victoria is Africa's largest lake by surface area, yet nearby Tanganyika holds much more water. Victoria spreads across a broad, comparatively shallow basin between branches of the East African Rift.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Vänern has salmon that spend their lives in fresh water. The lake preserves lineages stranded inland as the landscape changed after the last ice age.
options.label: Source

options.text: Ships from the sea can climb all the way to Vänern. Six locks on the route from Gothenburg lift them up to the lake.
options.label: Source

options.text: Sailing the Vänern archipelago takes you past more than bare rock. Some stretches of shore have drifting sand dunes, others wet meadows and fields of wave-worn stones.
options.label: Source

options.text: Vänern is Sweden's largest lake and Europe's third-largest by surface area. Both European lakes ahead of it, Ladoga and Onega, are in Russia.
options.label: smhi.se

options.text: Water reaching Mweru from Lake Bangweulu first travels south, away from its destination. The Luapula then curves around the wetlands and turns north toward Mweru along the Zambia–Congo border.
options.label: openjicareport.jica.go.jp

options.text: Mweru has a neighbour with nearly the same name and a connection that switches on and off. When Mweru Wantipa fills it can reach Lake Mweru through a swampy hollow. In dry periods the smaller lake can itself disappear.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Mifimbo is a protected fish breeding area on the Zambian side of Mweru. One small stretch of habitat helps replenish catches made across a much larger lake.
options.label: parliament.gov.zm

options.text: Most of the time, this long blue shape on a map of South Australia is a dry salt flat. Thunderstorms sometimes leave shallow patches of water on it.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: When rain filled Lake Torrens in 1989, banded stilts bred there. It was the first documented breeding of the species in South Australia since 1930.
options.label: Source

options.text: When Kokatha applicants sought heritage protection for Lake Torrens, they described the whole lake surface, islands included, as significant under Aboriginal tradition.
options.label: Source

options.text: Rain that reaches Lake Torrens usually has no river route to the sea. The water collects in a closed basin and leaves mainly by evaporation or seepage.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Issyk-Kul tastes slightly salty even though mountain streams feed it. Measurements put it at roughly six grams of salt per litre, well below ocean salinity.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: The basin drops more than six hundred metres below the lake surface. Snow peaks surround a body of water deeper than some seas.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Wintering waterbirds gather at Issyk-Kul high in the Tian Shan. Open water here provides a stopping place surrounded by frozen mountain country.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Issyk-Kul sits more than 1,600 metres above the sea, ringed by the Tian Shan. The rivers flowing down from those snowy peaks enter a basin with no surface outlet.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: The bridges on euro banknotes were imaginary when the notes were designed. Each represents an era of European architecture without giving one country’s landmark pride of place.
options.label: Source

options.text: The EU flag kept its twelve stars as countries joined. The circle represents unity, so you cannot count the member countries by counting the stars.
options.label: Source

options.text: The 1985 Schengen Agreement was signed on a riverboat on the Moselle. The village that gave open borders their name sits where Luxembourg, France and Germany meet.
options.label: Source

options.text: You can cross a land border from Brazil into the European Union. On the far bank of the Oyapock River is French Guiana, an EU region on the South American mainland.
options.label: cp-rup.com

options.text: The name Micronesia means “small islands”, but the islands come in very different heights. Volcanic high islands and low coral atolls share the regional name.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: Guam and the Marshall Islands lie in the same geographic region. Between them stretch the Caroline Islands, a reminder that Micronesia covers several separate chains.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: Banaba is an unusual Micronesian island. In a country otherwise made up of low atolls, this raised coral island carries an elevated plateau.
options.label: mfed.gov.ki

options.text: Micronesia's islands are scattered across an expanse comparable to Australia, but their combined land area is smaller than Rhode Island. Most of what the regional name covers is ocean.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: In Slovenia’s Kras region, the Reka River dives underground. Inside the Škocjan Caves it runs through a canyon whose roof in places is about 150 metres above the water.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: During carnival around Kastav in Croatia, groups in sheepskins walk from village to village with bells tied around their waists. The procession makes its own soundtrack as it moves.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Lake Ohrid, on the Albanian–North Macedonian border, drillers recovered hundreds of metres of lake mud. The record reaches back about 1.36 million years to when a permanent lake formed.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Balkans are easiest to outline from the sea. The Adriatic, Ionian, Aegean and Black seas mark the peninsula on three sides, while its northern edge runs across land.
options.label: cmes.arizona.edu

options.text: In 1976 Mau Piailug guided the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti. He followed the rising points of stars, the sun, moon and ocean swells across the equator.
options.label: Source

options.text: The ancestors of Māori carried kūmara to Aotearoa on their ocean voyages. Centuries later, archaeologists could still identify the crop from microscopic starch grains in old storage pits.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Rapa Nui, carvers shaped most moai from relatively soft volcanic tuff. The picks they used were themselves volcanic rock, made of much harder basalt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Three islands mark the corners of the Polynesian Triangle. Join Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa New Zealand on a Pacific map and much of Polynesia lies inside.
options.label: nzhistory.govt.nz

options.text: In Vanuatu, a sand artist can draw a whole symmetrical design with one finger in a continuous line. The guiding grid can exist entirely in the artist’s mind.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ancient ditches at Kuk in the highlands of New Guinea record an independent beginning of agriculture. By roughly 7,000 years ago, people were tending crops in what had been wetland.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Malaita in the Solomon Islands, craftspeople string polished pieces of shell into money. A fieldworker who watched a group making it recorded the songs the women sang as they worked.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The island of New Guinea runs across a boundary on regional maps. Its eastern part is Papua New Guinea in Melanesia, while the western part belongs to Indonesia in Southeast Asia.
options.label: unsdg.un.org

options.text: Along western Norway's fjords, a mountain valley can continue far below sea level. Glaciers cut the troughs deep enough for the sea to reach well into the mountains after the ice retreated.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the sandy tip of Denmark, waves from the Skagerrak and Kattegat meet from different directions. Sand carried along the coasts keeps reshaping the very point where the seas meet.
options.label: visitdenmark.com

options.text: Norway, Sweden and Finland meet at a point in a lake. A walkway leads out to the Three-Country Cairn, so you can walk around the marker and cross three national borders without getting wet.
options.label: kirunalapland.se

options.text: Surveyors used Europe itself as a measuring instrument. A chain of triangles ran more than 2,800 kilometres from northern Norway to the Black Sea to measure the shape of the Earth.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Europe’s southern gateway, two currents pass through Gibraltar in opposite directions. Atlantic water enters the Mediterranean at the surface while heavier, saltier water leaves underneath.
options.label: Source

options.text: An ocean once lay where the Alps now stand. Its seabed sank between converging plates before their collision pushed up the mountains.
options.label: Source

options.text: Europe and Asia share a continuous mainland. The conventional boundary crosses the Ural Mountains, so you can walk from one continent into the other without crossing any sea.
options.label: ipcc.ch

options.text: Utah's Great Salt Lake is a remnant of a much larger lake. On nearby mountainsides, old Lake Bonneville shorelines look like bathtub rings high above the modern valley floor.
options.label: geology.utah.gov

options.text: On Anticosti Island in Canada's St Lawrence, fossil-bearing beds record one of Earth's great mass extinctions. A walk along the exposed rock crosses layers laid down in an ancient sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Part of the Pacific Plate carries North American land. Baja California is moving with that plate as the Gulf of California opens between it and mainland Mexico.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: Some phosphorus feeding the Amazon comes from Africa. Satellites have tracked dust from the Sahara crossing the Atlantic and delivering the nutrient to the rainforest.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The ocean floor off South America is moving underneath the continent. Along the Andes, earthquakes trace the descent of the Nazca Plate into the Earth.
options.label: Source

options.text: High in the Chilean Andes, the air is dry enough for the ALMA telescopes to detect faint millimetre waves from cold clouds in space. Water vapour lower down would absorb much of that signal.
options.label: Source

options.text: The point on Earth's surface farthest from its centre is in South America. Ecuador's Chimborazo gets a head start over Everest because Earth bulges at the equator.
options.label: blogs.loc.gov

options.text: Water from the Tibetan highlands reaches seas on opposite sides of Asia. The Indus heads for the Arabian Sea, while the Yangtze crosses China toward the Pacific.
options.label: NASA

options.text: In Central Asia, irrigation diverted so much water from the rivers feeding the Aral Sea that a new desert appeared on the exposed lakebed.
options.label: Source

options.text: Papermaking changed as it travelled across Asia. In the region around Samarkand, makers turned rags into fine paper, adapting a craft that in China had used mulberry and bamboo.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Asia holds both ends of the land elevation scale. Everest's summit and the exposed shore of the Dead Sea are separated vertically by more than nine kilometres.
options.label: guinnessworldrecords.com

options.text: Fossils found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco put members of our own species in northwest Africa about 300,000 years ago.
options.label: Source

options.text: One of Africa’s great deltas floods in the dry season. Water flowing into Botswana’s Okavango spreads across an inland plain just when the surrounding landscape is drying out.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The chain of long lakes in eastern Africa marks a continent slowly pulling apart. Water has collected in the deep valleys formed as the crust stretched and faulted.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Africa is the only continent crossed by the equator, both tropics and the prime meridian. You can find all four of those lines on a single outline of its mainland.
options.label: anrseb.gov.et

options.text: About 94 per cent of the continent of Zealandia lies underwater. New Zealand is one of the places where you can stand on the small part above the Pacific.
options.label: Source

options.text: When sea levels fell during the ice ages, Australia, Tasmania and New Guinea were joined by dry land. The water gaps between them on a modern map came later.
options.label: Source

options.text: Māori voyaging ancestors could keep their bearings even when clouds hid the stars. Ocean swells and wind direction gave navigators another way to hold a course.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Pacific island's shape can tell you how it formed. Oceania contains steep volcanic high islands as well as low coral atolls that trace the rims of volcanoes now submerged.
options.label: education.nationalgeographic.org

options.text: In Patagonia’s Cave of the Hands, outlines of human fingers share the rock with pictures of hunters and guanacos. Guanacos still roam the landscape those artists knew thousands of years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Andean forests of northern Patagonia grows the alerce, a conifer whose lifespan can exceed 3,600 years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Buenos Aires, trucks and buses became canvases for filete porteño. Painters use long-haired brushes to combine elaborate lettering, bright colours and flourishes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Western Hemisphere's highest mountain and lowest exposed land are in the same country. Argentina contains both Aconcagua in the Andes and Laguna del Carbón in Patagonia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On the west coast, whale sharks gather each year above Ningaloo Reef. A few steps inland, the limestone landscape conceals a network of caves and underground waterways.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Limestone caves in the Tasmanian wilderness preserve traces of people who lived there more than 20,000 years ago, when ice still shaped the island’s gorges.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Blue Mountains contain more than ninety kinds of eucalypt. Their sandstone gullies and plateaux preserve a record of how this one group of trees diversified in Australia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Australia is the largest country without a land border. You could follow its entire mainland coast without ever crossing into another country.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Tsodilo, a patch of Kalahari Desert just ten square kilometres across contains more than 4,500 rock paintings. Local communities still regard the hills as sacred.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Veekuhane Seperu dance, a leader chooses a dancer with a flywhisk. She fans her layered skirt into a peacock’s tail as others imitate a dove.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wosana, a Bakalanga rainmaking tradition in Botswana, extends into villages across the Zimbabwean border. The gathering brings prayers, meals, songs and dancers together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Botswana has a great river delta without a coast. The Okavango fans out into the Kalahari, where most of its water evaporates or passes through plants instead of reaching an ocean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Khmer shadow-theatre puppet can stand two metres tall. For Sbek Thom, a craftsperson cuts an entire character out of a single piece of leather.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: After the fall of the Khmer Rouge in 1979, surviving dancers reassembled troupes and began performing Cambodia’s royal ballet repertoire again.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Preah Vihear, reaching the sanctuary means following some 800 metres of stairways and pavements to a temple on a cliff above the Cambodian plain.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Tonle Sap River changes direction with the seasons. When the Mekong rises, it pushes water upstream into Cambodia's great lake, which drains back towards the Mekong when the floods recede.
options.label: mrcmekong.org

options.text: At the northern tip of Newfoundland, archaeologists uncovered turf buildings like those in Iceland and Greenland. They mark an eleventh-century Norse settlement on the far side of the Atlantic.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Alberta’s Milk River Valley, Blackfoot artists engraved and painted the sandstone. The place is known as Áísínai’pi, or Writing-on-Stone.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Gros Morne in Newfoundland, you can stand on rock from Earth’s mantle. Pieces of the deep ocean floor and the rock beneath it were pushed up onto land.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The world's second-largest country has the world's longest coastline. Canada's map includes an immense Arctic archipelago as well as its Atlantic and Pacific shores.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In northeastern China, a dance of the Korean community takes its steps from farming. Dancers mime walking the ridges between fields to drums, gongs and the piercing sound of a suona.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Hunan’s Wulingyuan landscape, more than 3,000 sandstone pillars and peaks rise above the ravines. Many individual pillars are taller than 200 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional Chinese block printers prepare smooth planks of pear or jujube wood only two centimetres thick. An image starts on thin paper before an engraver cuts it into the wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: From the Pacific coast to the frontiers of Central Asia, clocks in China show the same official time. The country stretches across roughly five geographical time zones.
options.label: timeanddate.com

options.text: Listen to vallenato from the Magdalena region and you can hear several histories at once. Cattle herders’ songs, African chants, Indigenous dance rhythms and Spanish verse all helped shape it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A varnished wooden object from Pasto begins far from the woodshop. Harvesters collect buds in the forests of Putumayo to make the material decorators call mopa-mopa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Barranquilla’s four days of carnival reflect its past as a Caribbean trading port. Dance traditions from Colombia’s interior met European and African ones there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Colombia is the only South American country with both a Caribbean coast and a Pacific coast. Panama meets it at the narrow corner between the two.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Cuban son, the bass helps tell the dancers where to step. Musicians improvise around patterns, drawing lyrics from everyday life and passing songs on by ear.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: After upheavals in Haiti in the 1790s, enslaved people brought tumba francesa to eastern Cuba. Its dances joined French forms with musical traditions from West Africa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The palaces in Cuba’s city of Trinidad trace the fortunes of sugar. The Brunet and Cantero mansions date from the town’s prosperity in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean. Its long east–west axis separates the Straits of Florida in the north from much of the Caribbean Sea to the south.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Quito grew high in the Andes, at roughly 2,850 metres. An equatorial capital can have cool days because its streets are nearly three kilometres above sea level.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sangay National Park spans a steep slice of Ecuador from tropical foothills to high volcanic terrain. A short distance on the map covers an enormous change in altitude.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Galápagos sit where tectonic and volcanic activity keeps making new ground. The archipelago preserves islands at different stages in the life of a volcanic island chain.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The spot on Earth's surface farthest from its centre is in Ecuador. Chimborazo beats Everest on that measure because Earth bulges at the equator.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: At Abu Simbel, engineers cut rock temples into blocks and moved them uphill. The original site disappeared beneath the reservoir created by the Aswan High Dam.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mount Sinai rises on Egypt's Asian side. An ancient monastery at its foot stands in the rugged mountains of a country often pictured as a flat African desert.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Nile fans out into a broad triangle before it enters the Mediterranean. Much of Egypt's population occupies that delta and the narrow river valley leading to it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Egypt occupies the land bridge between Africa and Asia. At the isthmus, the Suez Canal cuts a sea-level route across the land and leaves the Sinai Peninsula on its Asian side.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Some of the last surviving traditional buildings of the Asante near Kumasi are made from earth, timber and straw. Keeping them standing means caring for materials the rains readily wear away.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A lead singer calls and a chorus answers in Ghanaian highlife. Guitars and horns can share the rhythm with drums and xylophones, in songs drawn from daily life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Ghanaian kente cloth can have a proverb for a name. Weavers make narrow strips on horizontal looms, choosing patterns and colours that can signal who will wear the fabric.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Volta covers more surface area than any other artificial reservoir built over a river valley. The Akosombo Dam flooded more than 8,000 square kilometres of Ghana.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Iceland acquired a new island within living memory. Surtsey rose out of the Atlantic in 1963, and scientists have tracked life colonising it ever since.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The rift at Þingvellir opens as the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart. On dry land you can walk among the cracks marking an ocean-spreading system.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Icelandic has a word for floods released from beneath glaciers, jökulhlaup. In Vatnajökull, heat from volcanoes beneath the ice can help unleash them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Reykjavík is the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state. Even so, it lies south of the Arctic Circle.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A national park in India floats. At Keibul Lamjao on Loktak Lake, mats of roots, vegetation and soil are thick enough to support grazing sangai deer.
options.label: incredibleindia.gov.in

options.text: Where India's Ganges delta meets the sea, tigers live among tidal mangrove islands. Channels fill and empty through the Sundarbans twice a day.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: India’s only active volcano is out at sea, well away from the Himalayas. Barren Island rises from the Andaman Sea on the volcanic arc that continues towards Indonesia.
options.label: prod.incredibleindia.gov.in

options.text: In Papua's Lorentz National Park, one protected area runs from tropical seas through swamps and forest to high alpine terrain. The change in climate happens on a single mountain slope.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Bali, irrigation associations called subak link rice terraces to water temples. Water flowing downhill connects fields owned by different farmers.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Komodo dragons live naturally on a small set of Indonesian islands. An animal large enough to dominate its landscape has a native range that fits into a tiny patch of the archipelago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The equator crosses several countries, but Indonesia has the largest land area of any country made up entirely of islands. Its territory stretches from Sumatra to the western half of New Guinea.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: An arc of sinkholes across the Yucatán traces the rim of a buried impact crater. Groundwater found weaknesses along the edge of Chicxulub, so the line of holes reveals a crater mostly hidden under younger rock.
options.label: lpi.usra.edu

options.text: In 1943 a Mexican farmer saw a volcano begin in a cornfield. Parícutin erupted for nine years, leaving a cone hundreds of metres tall where the field had been.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: Most of Baja California rides on the Pacific Plate while mainland Mexico lies on the North American Plate. The peninsula is slowly travelling northwest relative to the mainland across the Gulf of California.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: A high-resolution model of Earth’s gravity put its weakest pull at the surface near the top of Peru’s Huascarán. Its elevation and its position near the equator both help make gravity unusually weak there.
options.label: espace.curtin.edu.au

options.text: Ice in the tropical Andes preserves a year-by-year record of snowfall. Cores from Peru’s Quelccaya ice cap contain annual layers stretching back well over a thousand years.
options.label: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: Which Peruvian stream counts as the start of the Amazon depends on the question. Measurements along the Mantaro traced a longer route to the mouth than the traditional Apurímac source, but part of the Mantaro route can run dry.
options.label: rgs-ibg.onlinelibrary.wiley.com
