options.text: On Beqa, Sawau firewalkers trace their gift to an ancestor who went looking for an eel. In the story, the creature he caught could speak and offered him power over fire in return for its freedom.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Fijian drua carries its crew across the ocean on two hulls. The deck between them turns two slender canoe bodies into a platform for long-distance sailing.
options.label: Source

options.text: Fiji’s first colonial capital was Levuka on Ovalau. Its old port still follows the beach in a low line of buildings among mango and coconut trees.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Taveuni you can step across the 180th meridian between the eastern and western hemispheres. Both feet are still in Fiji, on the same calendar day.
options.label: fiji.travel

options.text: In the southern highlands, Huli men grew their own hair to make wigs. An example in Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum is decorated with everlasting flowers.
options.label: Source

options.text: A large Iatmul canoe on the Sepik often has a crocodile for a prow. The carver shapes the head directly at the front of the wooden vessel.
options.label: Source

options.text: Highland farmers at Kuk left their oldest field plans buried in a swamp. Their ditches and planting surfaces show that agriculture developed independently in New Guinea thousands of years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Follow the long spine of mountains across New Guinea and you cross an international border. Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern part of the island and Indonesia the west.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Sharks have been filmed swimming inside Kavachi, an active underwater volcano in the Solomon Islands. Researchers lowered a camera into the crater during a lull in eruptions.
options.label: tos.org

options.text: Tetepare is the largest uninhabited island in the South Pacific. Its former residents' descendants now help protect the forest that grew there.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: On Vangunu and New Georgia, the local fauna includes a monkey-faced flying fox. Despite the face and the name, the animal is a fruit bat.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: A Cook Islands tīvaevae in Te Papa’s collection has a design its maker used for seven wedding quilts. She changed the colours each time she sewed it.
options.label: Source

options.text: A travelling companion of Māori ancestors left a genetic trail across the Pacific. DNA from kiore, the Pacific rat, links early New Zealand populations with lineages in the Cook and Society islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Manihiki, one of the northern atolls, the lagoon serves as a farm. Cultivating oysters for pearls became one of the island’s principal commercial activities.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Cook Islands come in two very different groups. The northern islands are low coral atolls, while the south includes the high volcanic island of Rarotonga.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The country's highest summit, Nanlaud, is on Pohnpei. It rises more than 780 metres above the sea in a country that also has low coral islets.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The high islands can support streams, while people on low atolls depend on rainfall and thin freshwater lenses. Two islands in the same federation can have entirely different supplies of drinking water.
options.label: hawaii.edu

options.text: The federal capital, Palikir, is on Pohnpei. The country shares the name of the wider Micronesian region, but its capital governs only four island states within it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Four states share the country's 607 islands. From west to east they are Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, strung along the Caroline Islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Guam changes character halfway down the island. The north is a relatively level limestone plateau, while the south rises into rugged volcanic hills.
options.label: ghs.guam.gov

options.text: Much of northern Guam gets drinking water from a lens of fresh groundwater in limestone. Salt water lies underneath it, even inland from the shore.
options.label: epa.guam.gov

options.text: Mount Lamlam reaches only about 400 metres above sea level. The highest point on this island sits in the mountainous south.
options.label: ghs.guam.gov

options.text: The largest island in all of Micronesia sits at the southern tip of one island chain. Follow the Marianas south and the last island you reach is Guam.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Pentecost Island, the yam harvest is marked by land diving. Participants leap from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles.
options.label: Source

options.text: Oral traditions about Chief Roi Mata tie together three islands. Archaeologists found physical evidence at sites remembered as his home, the place he died and his burial ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A drawing in sand can cross a language boundary in Vanuatu. Communities speaking dozens of languages have shared a way of tracing patterns to communicate and pass on stories.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Plot Vanuatu's islands on a map and they form a Y. Some of the volcanoes in that chain never break the surface of the Pacific.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Taputapuātea on Raiatea, sacred gathering grounds face a lagoon and a passage through the reef. The site connected Polynesian communities whose visitors had to cross the ocean to meet.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Fakarava, thousands of camouflage groupers gather in a reef pass to spawn around the full moon. For a brief window, divers can see fish normally spread across the reef packed together.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1769 James Cook watched Venus cross the face of the Sun from Tahiti. His drawing records the planet as a little black disc against the bright Sun.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Tuamotus form the world's largest group of atolls. This one French Polynesian archipelago contains nearly eighty rings of coral.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Among Palau’s Rock Islands are lakes of seawater cut off from the open ocean. Some have developed their own distinctive jellyfish populations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Palauan bai is a meeting house that can also be read. Painted scenes on its timbers preserve stories for the people gathering beneath them.
options.label: Source

options.text: Palauan chiefs could declare a bul, closing an area to harvesting so it could recover. That customary practice helped shape the islands’ system of protected waters.
options.label: Source

options.text: Palau's Rock Islands have the world's highest concentration of marine lakes. Many of these pockets of seawater sit entirely inside islands and look like freshwater lakes from above.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Kiritimati is the world's largest coral atoll by land area. The measure matters because other atolls enclose much larger expanses of lagoon.
options.label: mfed.gov.ki

options.text: One of Kiribati's islands stands apart geologically. Banaba is raised coral, while the country's other 32 islands are classed as atolls.
options.label: mfed.gov.ki

options.text: Kiribati has three separate groups on a Pacific map. From west to east, its territory stretches through the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line islands.
options.label: mfed.gov.ki

options.text: Kiribati has land in all four hemispheres. Its islands lie on both sides of the equator and on both sides of the 180th meridian.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A Marshallese navigation chart records something a coastline map leaves out. Curved sticks show how ocean swells bend and cross around islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1946 a fleet of more than seventy ships lay anchored at Bikini Atoll as targets for a nuclear test. The lagoon became a graveyard for part of that fleet.
options.label: Source

options.text: To make a ceremonial dress mat called a jaki-ed, weavers boil and dry a particular kind of pandanus leaf. Beating it releases fibres fine enough to weave into clothing.
options.label: Source

options.text: At Kwajalein the lagoon covers roughly a hundred times as much area as the land around it. The enormous outline you see on a map is almost entirely seawater.
options.label: documents1.worldbank.org

options.text: Mining the phosphate from Nauru’s interior uncovered a forest of sharp limestone pinnacles. Much of the plateau was left too rugged for homes or farming.
options.label: Source

options.text: Nauruans have a tradition of catching and taming frigatebirds. These ocean-going birds, known locally as itsi, have a place in island life beyond their visits to the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Nauruan flag is a miniature map. The line marks the equator, the star sits south of it like the island, and its twelve points recall the traditional tribes.
options.label: Source

options.text: Nauru is the world's smallest island country. The only independent states with less land, Monaco and Vatican City, are both on the European mainland.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Before dawn, a kagu can announce itself with a bark. This grey, ground-dwelling bird lives wild only in New Caledonia.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonian crows make tools with hooks. Researchers watched wild birds fashion hooked implements and use them to reach food they could not grasp with their beaks.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonia’s barrier reefs enclose lagoons with room for dugongs. These plant-eating relatives of manatees live alongside turtles and whales in the reef system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Parts of New Caledonia have a double barrier reef. Heading out from the coast, a boat can pass one reef barrier and still have another between it and the open Pacific.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Niue gets rain but has no permanent rivers running across its surface. Water drains through the porous coral limestone that makes up the island.
options.label: Source

options.text: Niuean hiapo is cloth made from bark. Nineteenth-century artists drew fine designs on it freehand, turning the pale surface into an intricate patterned sheet.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Niuean fisher could head out in a small vaka with an outrigger for stability. A common form carries just one or two people along the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: Almost the entire coast of Niue is ringed by coral reef. The one major break is on the central west coast, where the island faces the afternoon sun.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A freshwater pool on Upolu sits almost at the edge of the Pacific. At Piula, spring water emerges from an old lava tube beside the sea, so a swimmer can go from fresh water to salt water in a few steps.
options.label: samoa.travel

options.text: Goldfish live in a volcanic crater high above the Pacific. They were introduced to Lake Lanotoʻo on Upolu, where their descendants still swim in a lake surrounded by rainforest.
options.label: samoa.travel

options.text: Savaiʻi rises from tropical beaches to a summit 1,858 metres above sea level. High on Mount Silisili the forest is often inside a cloud, on the very same island as the lowland coconut palms.
options.label: samoa.travel

options.text: On Tuvalu’s coral atolls, growers raise pulaka, a giant swamp taro, down in dug pits. The gardens bring its roots close to freshwater beneath the island surface.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tuvalu’s game of te ano is played with two balls. The hard balls are traditionally made from pandanus leaves.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the 1890s an expedition brought drilling equipment to Funafuti to test how coral atolls form. The layers beneath the island offered a way to investigate a question Darwin had raised.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tuvalu's nine islands show three different arrangements of water. Six have lagoons open to the ocean, two have enclosed lagoons, and Niulakita has none.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Daikoku, a submarine volcano in the Mariana arc, explorers found a pool of molten sulfur on the seafloor. Ordinary seawater flows over a liquid with a much higher melting point.
options.label: fisheries.noaa.gov

options.text: At the Champagne vent in the Mariana arc, the bubbles rising from the seabed contain liquid carbon dioxide. The pressure there is high enough to keep the gas in liquid form.
options.label: fisheries.noaa.gov

options.text: The Mariana Trench Marine National Monument has three distinct parts. One protects islands' surrounding waters, another protects volcanic sites, and a third follows the floor of the trench.
options.label: fisheries.noaa.gov

options.text: Tonga’s 2022 Hunga eruption sent a pressure wave ringing around Earth. Instruments continued to register its passage as it circled the globe over several days.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui on Tongatapu looks like a giant stone doorway. Its two upright posts and crosspiece are all slabs of coral limestone.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Tongan lakalaka is a speech you can watch. Performers stand in rows, singing and clapping while their movements deliver meaning alongside the words.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tonga's islands run in two parallel rows with different origins. Volcanoes built the western row, while coral limestone and sand make up the eastern islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: You can tell Wallis and Futuna apart by their reefs. Wallis has a broad lagoon behind a barrier reef with four passages, while Futuna has a reef fringing the shore and no comparable lagoon.
options.label: spccfpstore1.blob.core.windows.net

options.text: Alofi is only about 1.5 kilometres across the channel from Futuna. Almost nobody lives there permanently, but Futunans visit its Loka Cave on pilgrimage.
options.label: wallis-futuna.travel

options.text: Wallis and Futuna are often drawn as a pair of dots, yet about 230 kilometres of Pacific separate them. Futuna's mountainous skyline rises much higher than Wallis.
options.label: spccfpstore1.blob.core.windows.net

options.text: Traditional Hawaiian fishponds have a gate called a mākāhā. Water and small fish can pass between its slats, while larger fish stay in the pond.
options.label: Source

options.text: The mark between the last two vowels in Hawaiʻi is a consonant. Called the ʻokina, it signals a glottal stop. A line over a vowel, the kahakō, changes how long the vowel is held.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Hawaiian chain records the motion of an ocean plate. Volcanoes grow over a hot spot and are carried northwest, so islands farther along the chain are generally older.
options.label: Source

options.text: Everest has the higher summit, but Mauna Kea is taller from base to peak. Much of the Hawaiian volcano rises through the Pacific before it ever reaches sea level.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: Bagana builds its cone with thick lava that creeps down its flanks. Eruptions have been recorded on this Bougainville volcano since the nineteenth century.
options.label: Source

options.text: One variety of Rotokas, spoken on Bougainville, distinguishes just six consonant sounds. It is one of the smallest consonant inventories linguists have described.
options.label: Source

options.text: In bamboo bands on Bougainville and nearby Buka, players strike tuned tubes with rubber cut from footwear. A worn sandal can find a second life as a musical instrument.
options.label: Source

options.text: Bougainville is the largest island in the Solomon Islands archipelago, yet it belongs to Papua New Guinea. The political border crosses the island chain rather than enclosing it.
options.label: abg.gov.pg

options.text: Walk along the Jurassic Coast from west to east and the exposed rocks generally get younger. In one stretch of shore you can cross the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
options.label: unesco.org.uk

options.text: Hot springs determined where the Romans built the baths at Bath. Geothermal water still reaches the surface in the middle of the city.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Water power helped set the pattern of settlement in the Derwent Valley. Early cotton mills rose along the river, with workers' housing built near the machinery.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Stand on the brass line at Greenwich and a GPS receiver will put you slightly west of zero longitude. The modern reference meridian runs about 102 metres east of the historic one.
options.label: rmg.co.uk

options.text: On Staffa, the sea has cut Fingal's Cave into a wall of basalt columns. The columns grew as lava cooled and cracked, leaving what looks like a built arcade.
options.label: nts.org.uk

options.text: Scotland’s Loch Ness holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined. Its great depth matters more than its rather narrow outline.
options.label: environment.gov.scot

options.text: Shetland is closer to Bergen in Norway than to Edinburgh. The journey from these Scottish islands to their own capital is longer than the crossing to Scandinavia.
options.label: shetland.org

options.text: Rathlin's West Lighthouse has its lamp below the keepers' accommodation. The cliff is so high that putting the lamp at the top would have made it harder to see beneath low cloud.
options.label: irishlights.ie

options.text: Many islands in Strangford Lough are the tops of drumlins. The sea flooded a field of rounded hills moulded by ice, leaving their summits above the tide.
options.label: daera-ni.gov.uk

options.text: Three streams disappear into the limestone beneath County Fermanagh. Their waters come together underground in the Marble Arch Caves and reappear as the River Cladagh.
options.label: marblearchcaves.co.uk

options.text: On Yr Wyddfa, the highest mountain in Wales, the rocks contain fossils of sea creatures. What is now a summit once lay beneath an ancient sea.
options.label: geolsoc.org.uk

options.text: Skomer Island is full of seabirds you could easily miss by daylight. Manx shearwaters breed in burrows and usually come ashore under cover of darkness.
options.label: naturalresources.wales

options.text: The tide takes different lengths of time to travel around the two ends of Anglesey. In the Menai Strait between the island and mainland Wales, the resulting difference in water level helps drive the fierce currents of the Swellies.
options.label: v13.walescoastpath.gov.uk

options.text: People were mining salt near Hallstatt in the second millennium BCE. The town beside the lake owes much of its wealth to the mountain behind it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Semmering Railway crosses the Alps on viaducts and through tunnels laid out in the 1800s, while steam locomotives were still a young invention.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Vienna's Spanish Riding School passes on its work with Lipizzaner horses through generations of riders. Learning includes caring for the horses as well as riding them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The world's longest known ice cave is inside an Austrian mountain near Salzburg. Eisriesenwelt extends for more than 40 kilometres through the rock, with permanent ice near its entrance.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: More than thirty granite cairns mark Bronze Age burials at Sammallahdenmäki. People piled those stones up more than three thousand years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fiddlers in Kaustinen pass dance tunes on by ear. Several hundred local tunes belong to a tradition more than 250 years old.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Finnish has a word for the steam that rises when water hits hot sauna stones. Löyly is central to what makes a sauna a sauna.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Finland's Kvarken Archipelago, new land is still emerging from the Baltic. As the crust rebounds from the last ice sheet, islands grow together and bays turn into lakes.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Ireland has a broad central lowland ringed by uplands near the coast. Its outline of mountains is almost the reverse of an island with a single high mountain in the middle.
options.label: dfa.ie

options.text: The Shannon flows through a succession of lakes before opening into a long Atlantic estuary. Ireland's longest river is a freshwater route through much of the island's interior.
options.label: dfa.ie

options.text: Ireland's harp is played as well as worn as an emblem. Irish harpers keep alive distinct traditions of plucking metal strings with fingernails or other strings with fingertips.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ireland has lakes that vanish through the floor. In a turlough, rising groundwater floods a limestone hollow and then drains back underground, leaving a field where the lake was.
options.label: gsi.ie

options.text: The jagged towers of the Dolomites preserve ancient marine environments. Rocks that record tropical seas now stand thousands of metres up in the Italian Alps.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Italy's Aeolian Islands gave volcanology two technical terms. The names of Vulcano and Stromboli live on in descriptions of Vulcanian and Strombolian eruptions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mount Etna is an active volcano on the island of Sicily. People have recorded its eruptions across more than two thousand years, an unusually long written history for a volcano.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Two independent countries fit entirely inside Italy. Vatican City is enclosed by Rome, while San Marino is surrounded by Italian territory near the Adriatic.
options.label: civil-protection-knowledge-network.europa.eu

options.text: A canal dug in 1842 lowered Lake Engure by draining water into the Gulf of Riga. The exposed lake bed became new land along the shores of what had once been a Baltic lagoon.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Latvia’s largest lake is surprisingly thin. Lubāns averages only about 1.6 metres deep, and kilometres of embankments hold its waters apart from the surrounding lowlands.
options.label: bef.lv

options.text: One river links three countries under two familiar names. The Western Dvina rises in Russia and crosses Belarus, then flows through Riga as the Daugava before entering the Baltic.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: The top of the Naafkopf belongs to three countries. At its summit a hiker can step from Liechtenstein into Austria or Switzerland without descending the mountain.
options.label: en.tourismus.li

options.text: In 1927 the Rhine broke through its bank near Schaan. Much of Liechtenstein’s northern valley floor became a lake, with the mountain villages looking down on flooded settlements below.
options.label: e-archiv.li

options.text: Liechtenstein’s only railway is a nine-kilometre middle section of a line between two other countries. A train from Feldkirch in Austria to Buchs in Switzerland crosses Liechtenstein on the way.
options.label: Government of Liechtenstein

options.text: Lithuania's biggest river breaks into branches before reaching the Curonian Lagoon. Between the branches lies Rusnė Island, with some of the country's lowest ground.
options.label: vstt.lrv.lt

options.text: At Žuvintas, mats of reeds and other vegetation can form floating islands. The shallow lake is gradually turning into marsh around its edges.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: One calculation puts the geographical centre of Europe in Lithuania, north of Vilnius. The answer depends on where you draw Europe’s edges and which islands you include.
options.label: govilnius.lt

options.text: Luxembourg has two distinct landscapes with distinct names. The northern Oesling belongs to the Ardennes, while the lower Gutland spreads across the south.
options.label: luxembourg.public.lu

options.text: Part of Luxembourg's eastern edge follows the Moselle. The river valley makes a narrow wine-growing strip along the German border.
options.label: luxembourg.public.lu

options.text: Luxembourg has three neighbours touching its small territory. Travel clockwise from the west and you pass Belgium, Germany and France without encountering a coast.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Along much of Luxembourg's border with Germany, the boundary is the entire river. The two countries share sovereignty over the water rather than drawing a line down the middle.
options.label: act.public.lu

options.text: Water leaves Lake Prespa without using a visible river. Some seeps through limestone beneath the Galičica mountains and emerges at springs feeding the lower Lake Ohrid.
options.label: unece.org

options.text: North Macedonia's only natural lake island is in Prespa. Golem Grad lies close to the point where North Macedonia, Albania and Greece meet in the lake.
options.label: parksdinarides.org

options.text: North Macedonia has a hillside of natural stone figures. At Kuklica, erosion wore away soft material around harder caps, leaving a crowd of tall pillars known as the Stone Dolls.
options.label: portal.mdt.gov.mk

options.text: Malta once had elephants small enough to live on an island with little food. A cave called Għar Dalam preserved the bones of dwarf elephants and hippos, animals you might never associate with Malta today.
options.label: heritagemalta.mt

options.text: Gozo has an Inland Sea that fits inside a small hollow behind a cliff. Boats can leave the sheltered lagoon through a narrow natural tunnel and emerge in the open Mediterranean.
options.label: visitmalta.co.uk

options.text: Malta is the smallest EU member by land area. You could fit its entire archipelago into Luxembourg, the next smallest member, more than eight times.
options.label: European Union

options.text: At Old Orhei the Răut River bends around tall limestone promontories. Cliffs that the river carved became sites for caves, settlements and monasteries.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Moldova's highest ground, Dealul Bălănești, reaches only about 430 metres. The land falls to just a few metres above sea level along the Dniester.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Prut follows Moldova's western edge beside Romania. Farther east the Dniester takes a separate course towards the Black Sea, so the country sits between two different river systems.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Landlocked Moldova has a port that can receive seagoing ships. At Giurgiulești, a tiny stretch of Danube frontage connects the country to the Black Sea.
options.label: ebrd.com

options.text: Monaco holds a particular geographical distinction. It takes up less land than any other country with a coast.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A Genoese fortress built in 1215 stood on the rock of Monaco. The Grimaldis first captured it in 1297, more than a century before securing it for good.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Although French is widely spoken in Monaco, the official words of its national anthem are in Monégasque.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Monaco grew a new neighbourhood out into the Mediterranean. The six hectares of Mareterra added about three per cent to the entire country's land area.
options.label: eme.gouv.mc

options.text: Ada Bojana has three watery edges. Two are branches of the Bojana River, while the third is a sandy Adriatic beach.
options.label: montenegro.travel

options.text: Biogradska Gora preserves old-growth forest in Montenegro's mountains. Trees that escaped cutting surround a lake scooped out by a glacier.
options.label: montenegro.travel

options.text: The Tara has cut a canyon as much as 1,300 metres deep. The river then joins the Piva to form a new river, the Drina, on its way towards the Danube.
options.label: montenegro.travel

options.text: In Franeker a wool worker built a working model of the solar system into the ceiling of his living room. Eise Eisinga's planets still move.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Schokland used to be an island in the Zuiderzee. Drainage left it stranded in the middle of farmland.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The windmills at Kinderdijk helped keep farmland dry. They lifted water in stages so it could drain out when the river level allowed.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Only about half of the European Netherlands rises more than a metre above sea level. Roughly a quarter of its land is actually below it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Rjukan and Notodden, Norwegian waterfalls helped make fertiliser. Hydroelectricity powered factories that drew nitrogen from the air.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the rocks around Alta Fjord, generations of people painted and engraved thousands of images over a span of several millennia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Urnes, Viking carving traditions and Romanesque church architecture meet in one building made of wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Norway put a 24.5-kilometre road inside a mountain between Lærdal and Aurland. The Lærdal Tunnel is the world's longest road tunnel.
options.label: vegvesen.no

options.text: Prehistoric miners at Krzemionki dug shafts and galleries in search of striped flint. Some of what they mined became polished axe heads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Tarnowskie Góry, water pumped out to keep the mines dry found a second use. It supplied drinking water to people above ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Two Lutheran Churches of Peace in Silesia rank as Europe's largest timber-framed religious buildings. They grew out of the settlement that ended the Thirty Years' War.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Poland has a patch of bare sand called the Błędów Desert. Centuries of cutting down forest for nearby mines exposed the sand well inland from the Baltic coast.
options.label: visitmalopolska.pl

options.text: Some of the enormous waves at Nazaré owe their height to a canyon hidden under the sea. The abrupt change in water depth concentrates incoming Atlantic swell near the Portuguese coast.
options.label: doi.org

options.text: Part of Portugal rides on the North American Plate. Flores and Corvo, the two westernmost Azorean islands, lie across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge from the main group.
options.label: academic.oup.com

options.text: Glaciers once carved valleys into mainland Portugal’s highest mountains. Serra da Estrela preserves U-shaped valleys and high peat bogs far to the south of Europe’s familiar glacial landscapes.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: At Buzău, Romania has volcanoes that erupt cool mud. Gas rising through wet sediments pushes mud to the surface and builds small cones.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: A cave in Romania contains a glacier underground. In Scărișoara, cold air descends into a deep hollow and helps preserve a thick block of ice through the summer.
options.label: digitalcommons.usf.edu

options.text: South of Romania’s Danube Delta, a former arm of the Black Sea became a string of lagoons. River sediment and coastal sand barriers helped cut the Razim–Sinoe waters off from the open sea.
options.label: pdf.usaid.gov

options.text: On the Lena River in Siberia, water works like a wedge. Repeated freezing and thawing helped separate cliffs into ranks of enormous stone pillars.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A major wild reindeer migration crosses the Putorana Plateau, where Arctic tundra and northern forest meet above the Arctic Circle.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ice Age artists in Shulgan-Tash Cave painted a two-humped camel alongside mammoths and woolly rhinoceroses in what is now the southern Urals.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Russia stretches so far around the Arctic that part of its mainland crosses 180° longitude. The far eastern tip of Siberia is in the Western Hemisphere.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: San Marino has only one neighbouring country, yet you can leave it for two different Italian regions. Emilia-Romagna lies on one side and Marche on the other.
options.label: visitsanmarino.com

options.text: San Marino is Europe’s third-smallest country by area. At roughly 61 square kilometres, it is still more than twenty times the size of Monaco and Vatican City put together.
options.label: dfat.gov.au

options.text: Marine fossils have been found on Mount Titano. The rock of this landlocked country's most recognisable mountain preserves animals from an ancient sea.
options.label: educazione.sm

options.text: Slovak shepherds played a flute about as tall as a person. The fujara can be two metres long, yet its player uses just three finger holes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Slovak wireworkers once repaired cracked household pots by binding them in wire. The repair technique grew into a decorative craft of its own.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Banská Štiavnica a mining town reshaped its watershed. Reservoirs and channels collected the water that helped power its mining machinery.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bratislava's municipal limits touch two foreign countries. At the city's southwestern edge, Slovakia, Austria and Hungary meet at one point.
options.label: visitbratislava.com

options.text: At Lake Cerknica, the same ground can be a lake one season and a meadow another. Water fills the karst basin faster than it drains through holes in its floor.
options.label: notranjski-park.si

options.text: Slovenia’s short Adriatic shore has the northernmost salt pans in the Mediterranean where salt is still harvested in the traditional way. Seawater passes through shallow basins and the sun does the concentrating.
options.label: slovenia.si

options.text: In the limestone beneath Slovenia lives a salamander that keeps its gills as an adult. The olm spends its life in groundwater and can survive for years between meals.
options.label: slovenia.info

options.text: Spain reaches its highest point off the African coast. Teide on Tenerife rises above every summit on the Spanish mainland.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A piece of Spain sits entirely inside France. To drive from the Spanish town of Llívia to the rest of Spain, you cross a strip of French territory in the Pyrenees.
options.label: treaties.un.org

options.text: A desert in southern Spain is shaped by running water. Most of the year the channels at Tabernas stand dry, but sudden downpours carry enough mud and stone to carve deep gullies.
options.label: juntadeandalucia.es

options.text: In Kiruna, an iron ore mine is changing the street map above it. In 2025 the town's wooden church was moved in one piece away from ground affected by mining.
options.label: lkab.com

options.text: Sweden’s highest point changed peaks as a glacier melted. Kebnekaise’s ice-capped southern summit lost enough height for its rocky northern neighbour to overtake it.
options.label: natgeo.su.se

options.text: A lake in central Sweden curves around the scar of an asteroid impact. Lake Siljan occupies part of the ring-shaped depression left after rock rebounded at the centre of the crater.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: A train can cross the Swiss Alps without climbing to a high pass. The Gotthard Base Tunnel takes a 57-kilometre route through the mountain at a much lower elevation.
options.label: uvek.admin.ch

options.text: Basel’s airport lies entirely in France, yet passengers can leave it directly for Switzerland. A special road links its Swiss sector to the border.
options.label: euroairport.com

options.text: Two differently coloured rivers meet in Geneva. The Rhône has passed through a lake where sediment settles, while the Arve brings cloudy water down from the Alps. Their colours stay distinct past the junction.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Ukraine’s Snake Island has territorial waters of its own. Yet when the international court drew the offshore boundary with Romania in 2009, it gave the island no extra reach beyond that belt. One island had two very different effects on the same maritime map.
options.label: legal.un.org

options.text: Southern Ukraine preserves a patch of European grassland that has never been ploughed. At Askania-Nova the original feather-grass steppe survived while agriculture transformed much of the plain around it.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Rain falling on opposite sides of Ukraine’s Carpathians can meet again hundreds of kilometres away. The Tisza drains one slope and the Prut another, but both eventually join the Danube.
options.label: davr.gov.ua

options.text: The Vatican Gardens cover about 22 hectares. Roughly half the territory of an entire country is set aside as gardens.
options.label: museivaticani.va

options.text: Some papal properties well outside Vatican City have extraterritorial privileges in Italy. The Lateran complex across Rome is one example, so a map of Vatican City alone leaves out part of the Holy See’s geographic footprint.
options.label: vatican.va

options.text: The World Heritage listing for Vatican City takes in the entire state. A single entry encompasses a country's boundary as well as its basilica, palaces and gardens.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Water entering Kosovo's Nerodimka river system can leave for two different seas. One branch feeds the Danube and Black Sea, the other the Vardar and Aegean.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Kosovo adopted a wordless anthem in 2008 so choosing lyrics would not privilege one ethnic community over another.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Gračanica and other medieval church sites in Kosovo, Byzantine and western Romanesque traditions meet in the architecture and painted interiors.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Landlocked Kosovo sends river water to three seas. Its watersheds feed the Adriatic to the west, the Black Sea to the north and the Aegean to the south.
options.label: documents1.worldbank.org

options.text: Flores and Corvo are politically Portuguese but ride on the North American tectonic plate. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs between these two islands and the rest of the Azores.
options.label: d197for5662m48.cloudfront.net

options.text: Santa Maria has seashells embedded in rock high above the Atlantic. Parts of the island were once submerged, then rose again carrying fossil-bearing stretches of ancient seabed with them.
options.label: parquesnaturais.azores.gov.pt

options.text: Off São Miguel, a rocky islet encloses an almost circular pool. Its walls are the remains of a volcanic crater, and a breach lets the Atlantic in and out.
options.label: visitportugal.com

options.text: Gibraltar's Gorham's Cave complex preserves traces of Neanderthal life on the Mediterranean coast. The Rock sheltered people long before anyone fortified it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Gibraltar's name recalls a person. Jabal Tariq, or Tariq's mountain, refers to the commander who took the peninsula in 711.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 transferred Gibraltar from Spain to Britain. The territory sits at the narrow passage between Atlantic and Mediterranean waters.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: An ancient sand dune climbs roughly 300 metres up the eastern face of the Rock of Gibraltar. What looks like a mountainside preserves sand piled up when the coastline lay farther out.
options.label: gibmuseum.gi

options.text: Victor Hugo made his home in exile at Hauteville House on Guernsey. He designed its extraordinary interiors and worked on Les Misérables there.
options.label: www.maisonsvictorhugo.paris.fr

options.text: Guernsey's Little Chapel is covered in pieces of broken china, pebbles and shells. Even its tiny passages are part of the mosaic.
options.label: www.visitguernsey.com

options.text: Saint Peter Port and Saint Peter in the Wood both honour the patron saint of fishermen. Their names tell you which parish faces the harbour.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Lihou becomes a walking destination and then an island again within one tide. Its stone causeway to Guernsey emerges only when the sea falls far enough.
options.label: biologicalrecordscentre.gov.gg

options.text: On Tynwald Hill, the island's parliament still holds an outdoor sitting. New laws are proclaimed in Manx and English.
options.label: www.tynwald.org.im

options.text: Manx is spoken again by children on the Isle of Man, following a revival that continued after the last traditional native speaker died.
options.label: courier.unesco.org

options.text: Off the island's southwestern tip sits a much smaller island with a fitting name, the Calf of Man. It is a sanctuary for birds.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Snaefell is the island's only summit over 2,000 feet. On a sufficiently clear day, people on top can look across the Irish Sea towards England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
options.label: visitisleofman.com

options.text: At La Cotte de St Brélade, a ravine in the coastal cliffs preserves Neanderthal occupation. During colder periods the sea retreated, putting today's seaside site well inland.
options.label: jerseyheritage.org

options.text: Jersey is the largest and southernmost of the Channel Islands. A map centred on Britain can disguise just how close the island lies to France.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Jersey's protected wetlands extend well offshore. Rocky outliers such as Les Écréhous emerge from a much larger area of reef and sand exposed at low tide.
options.label: gov.je

options.text: At a large spring tide, Jersey's exposed area can nearly double between high and low water. Reefs and broad shelves of seabed briefly become part of the island.
options.label: jersey.com

options.text: Madeira preserves a large surviving stretch of the laurel forest that once spread widely through southern Europe. Mist helps sustain it in the island's mountains.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some of Madeira's walking trails follow levadas. These narrow channels move water across the mountains to land that needs irrigation.
options.label: www.visitmadeira.com

options.text: On the steep streets below Monte, two runners steer a wicker sledge downhill on wooden runners. The ride began as a form of local transport.
options.label: visitmadeira.com

options.text: Madeira's coastal plain ran out before its airport runway did. Engineers carried part of the runway on a platform supported by great concrete columns beside the sea.
options.label: madeiracentral.com

options.text: The small island of Asinara off Sardinia is home to white donkeys. Their pale coats and eyes are the result of albinism.
options.label: parcoasinara.org

options.text: Sardinia is dotted with reservoirs, yet Baratz is its only natural freshwater lake. High dunes separate it from the Mediterranean a short distance away.
options.label: sardegnaturismo.it

options.text: On Sardinia a stream has carved a gorge hundreds of metres deep and only a few metres wide in places. In the Gorropu canyon, much of the water can vanish into the limestone below the boulder floor.
options.label: sardegnasentieri.it

options.text: The Sambian Peninsula juts into the Baltic between two lagoons. On a map, its blunt head separates the thin Vistula and Curonian spits.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Kaliningrad city sits inland from the open Baltic on the Pregolya River. Ships reach it through the lagoon west of the city.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The narrow Curonian Spit has two very different shores. Waves from the open Baltic break on one side, while shallow lagoon water laps against the other.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kaliningrad is on the Baltic yet has no land connection to the rest of Russia. Its only land neighbours are Poland and Lithuania.
options.label: lrt.lt

options.text: Etna's long record of observed eruptions stretches back millennia. Its slopes have helped scientists work out how volcanoes behave.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The floors of Villa Romana del Casale preserve an immense collection of Roman mosaics. A visitor can follow scenes across room after room of the villa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eight towns in southeastern Sicily were rebuilt after the earthquake of 1693. The disaster left an entire region with a recognisably Baroque face.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island, but the bottleneck separating it from mainland Italy is only about three kilometres across.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: The Åland Islands are part of Finland, but Swedish is their sole official language. The archipelago also has its own autonomous government and is demilitarised.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: The four-masted Pommern in Mariehamn harbour once carried grain from Australia to England under sail.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: Åland is still growing out of the Baltic. Its highest ground emerged around ten thousand years ago as the land rose after the ice sheets retreated.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: Finland and Sweden bend their border around a lighthouse on tiny Märket. A land swap kept the Finnish-built lighthouse on the Finnish side without changing either country's coastline.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: The Bzyb River helped build Cape Pitsunda by delivering sediment to the Black Sea. A flood can change where the river enters the sea and which stretches of beach receive fresh material.
options.label: environmentandsociety.org

options.text: A landslide in the mountains of Abkhazia dammed a valley and created Lake Ritsa. The water backed up behind fallen rock in a basin now surrounded by forested peaks.
options.label: dspace.nplg.gov.ge

options.text: Dye tracing in the Arabika limestone has connected high mountain caves to springs near the Black Sea coast. Water can descend an enormous vertical distance while barely appearing at the surface.
options.label: uis-speleo.org

options.text: A drowned river valley helped create the Iagorlîc reserve. Its quiet backwater, dry steppe slopes and woodland meet within a small stretch of Transnistria.
options.label: moldpres.md

options.text: A ravine near Tiraspol preserved an Ice Age menagerie. Fossils from its ancient river deposits include elephants, rhinoceroses, bison and hyenas from a landscape unlike today’s Dniester valley.
options.label: muzeu.md

options.text: The Dniester once offered migrating fish a route inland from the Black Sea. The dam at Dubăsari cut that route across the river, dividing habitats that had been connected through Transnistria.
options.label: ibn.idsi.md

options.text: Two lakes in the Corsican mountains sit on steps left by glaciers. Water from high Lake Capitello passes down to Lake Melo and into the Restonica valley on this Mediterranean island.
options.label: visit-corsica.com

options.text: The Gulf of Porto's reddish cliffs enclose nesting sites for ospreys. The birds fish where the island's volcanic headlands meet the Mediterranean.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Corsica's GR20 crosses the island diagonally from Calenzana to Conca. Walkers spend much of a Mediterranean island crossing up in the mountains, far above the beaches.
options.label: visit-corsica.com

options.text: Fossil leaves in Svalbard record a much warmer Arctic. Forests once grew in a place where the modern vegetation barely rises above the tundra.
options.label: svalbardmuseum.no

options.text: Some hills in Adventdalen have ice at their core. Groundwater freezes beneath the surface and pushes up a mound called a pingo.
options.label: doi.org

options.text: At Longyearbyen, winter darkness has a counterpart in summer. For months the Sun circles the sky without setting, even at local midnight.
options.label: en.visitsvalbard.com

options.text: In Istanbul, water can pass through the Bosporus in opposite directions at the same time. Less salty Black Sea water flows south at the surface while denser water from the Sea of Marmara flows north underneath.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: Turkey’s highest mountain is a volcano beside the borders of Armenia and Iran. Its two cones are so different in height that the summit of Little Ararat lies more than a kilometre below Great Ararat.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: NASA studied a Turkish lake to understand a crater on Mars. The pale mineral deposits around Lake Salda are a rare Earth counterpart to the carbonate deposits in Jezero crater, where the Perseverance rover landed.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In a Cypriot tsiattista duel the competitors improvise verses at each other. A quick answer has to fit the rhythm as well as land its point.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The plain exteriors of churches in the Troodos Mountains hide walls covered in Byzantine paintings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Lefkara, needleworkers build lace patterns by drawing threads out of linen and embroidering directly into the open spaces.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Cyprus you can walk uphill through ancient ocean floor. The Troodos Mountains expose a slice of oceanic crust and upper mantle lifted above the Mediterranean.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In the gorge at Tamgaly, people carved thousands of images into rock outcrops. Some of the open-air panels served pastoral communities moving through the dry landscape.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The mausoleum at Turkistan was left partly unfinished after Timur died. Its enormous brick dome still marks a city on the old caravan routes of Central Asia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kazakhstan's Caspian shore includes depressions well below sea level. At the opposite end of the country the Tian Shan climbs to around seven kilometres above it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, yet it has a long coastline. Its ports face the Caspian, a lake with no natural outlet to the ocean.
options.label: worldbank.org

options.text: Parts of western Bahrain are covered in prehistoric burial mounds. Nearly 12,000 survive in the listed fields, and some royal tombs had two storeys.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bahrain's pearling crews left behind a musical tradition called fjiri. Among its percussion instruments is a clay pot.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bahrain's old pearl route connects oyster beds offshore with merchants' houses in Muharraq. Following it takes you from the seabed to the people who sold the pearls.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Fresh water once bubbled up from the seabed off Bahrain. Submarine springs helped sustain an island trading centre in the salty waters of the Persian Gulf.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In Dhaka, a pedal rickshaw doubles as a moving painting. Artists decorate the vehicles by hand, turning ordinary journeys into a street exhibition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Jamdani weavers create motifs as they weave the cloth, adding individual threads into fine cotton by hand.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Dhaka's Bengali New Year procession grew out of an initiative by art students. Large colourful figures move through the streets with the marchers.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Three great rivers meet on the way out of Bangladesh. The Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna build the world's largest river delta where they reach the Bay of Bengal.
options.label: blogs.worldbank.org

options.text: In Kampong Ayer much of town life takes place above the Brunei River. Homes stand on stilts and people get around by walkways and water taxis.
options.label: www.bruneitourism.com

options.text: A strip of Malaysia divides Brunei in two. Temburong, the eastern part, has no land connection to the rest of the country within Brunei's borders.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Brunei's sultans once ruled far beyond the little state on today's map. Their influence extended from northwest Borneo into the southern Philippines.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Brunei connected the two pieces of its country by building across its own bay. Motorists can now reach Temburong without the four border checks on the old route through Malaysia.
options.label: bimp-eaga.asia

options.text: High Island's enormous hexagonal rock columns began in a volcano. They formed as hot volcanic material cooled and contracted.
options.label: www.geopark.gov.hk

options.text: Hong Kong includes more than two hundred islands as well as a piece of mainland China. Hong Kong Island itself is only one part of the territory.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The territory Britain acquired in 1842 was just Hong Kong Island. Kowloon was added later, and the New Territories came under a 99-year lease.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Hong Kong made room for its airport by reshaping the map. Builders levelled Chek Lap Kok and its smaller neighbour and joined them with land reclaimed from the sea.
options.label: hongkongairport.com

options.text: The Trans-Iranian Railway crosses two mountain ranges to join the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf. Its route runs through four climatic zones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pattern of caravanserais across Iran traces where travellers could find water and safety. These inns made long journeys by caravan possible.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Hawraman, terraced villages cling to the Zagros Mountains. The steep slopes shaped both the architecture and seasonal movements of the people living there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Iran's Lut Desert can be hotter than the hottest weather report. Satellite instruments have measured the land surface above 70°C there; weather stations measure the cooler air above it.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Makhtesh Ramon looks like an impact crater, but water carved it. Erosion removed softer rock from inside a fold and left a long hollow enclosed by cliffs.
options.label: static.parks.org.il

options.text: In Israel's Hula Valley, a drained wetland became a place to restore water. Migrating birds stop here on the overland route between Eurasia and Africa.
options.label: en.parks.org.il

options.text: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake whose surface is more than 200 metres below the Mediterranean. The Jordan River leaves it and flows farther downhill to the Dead Sea.
options.label: gov.il

options.text: Between Iraq’s two great rivers sits a lake filled from just one of them. Floodwater diverted from the Tigris spreads across the natural hollow of Lake Tharthar before it can reach Baghdad.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In little more than a decade, satellite images of southern Iraq went from green marsh to bare earth and back towards green. Drainage works emptied vast wetlands, then breaches in the embankments let river water return.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Ancient Ur now stands in dry country, but archaeologists have traced old watercourses around it. Mapping the vanished channels helps explain how such a large city could live there.
options.label: journals.uchicago.edu

options.text: Baengnyeong belongs to South Korea, yet the mainland you see from the island is North Korea. Its ferry connection to the South Korean mainland is much longer than the crossing to that nearby shore.
options.label: english.visitkorea.or.kr

options.text: A single county off southwestern South Korea contains roughly a thousand islands. In Sinan, the great expanses of mud you see between islands at low tide disappear beneath the sea twice a day.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Sunrise Peak on Jeju started as a separate island. A volcanic eruption through shallow seawater built the cone, and sediment later joined it to the much larger island beside it.
options.label: english.visitkorea.or.kr

options.text: At Mundok, the outgoing tide exposes a feeding stop on the flight between Australasia and Arctic breeding grounds. Migrating shorebirds use mudflats where two North Korean rivers reach the Yellow Sea.
options.label: neaspec.org

options.text: China comes close to the Sea of Japan along the Tumen River, yet the river mouth lies between North Korea and Russia. The two countries share a short stretch of frontier downstream of their meeting point with China.
options.label: static.un.org

options.text: The 38th parallel does not follow today's Korean border. Kaesong, now a North Korean city, lies south of that line.
options.label: history.army.mil

options.text: Wadi Mujib cuts through so much relief that one nature reserve stretches from below sea level near the Dead Sea to mountain country far above it. Different climates sit just a few kilometres apart.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Jordan has a single outlet to the open sea, but shares its gulf with three other countries. Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia all have coastline on the narrow Gulf of Aqaba.
options.label: mptf.undp.org

options.text: Some of the bridges in Jordan’s Wadi Rum are part of the mountains themselves. Weathering carved openings through sandstone ridges while leaving spans of rock high above the desert floor.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Seasonal sea ice reaches the Shiretoko Peninsula on Hokkaido. The ice helps feed a marine food web along a forested Japanese coast.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: At high tide, the buildings of Itsukushima Shrine appear to float. The shrine stands on pillars at the water's edge, so the tide changes how it looks without moving the buildings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Villages in Shirakawa-go and Gokayama have farmhouses with unusually steep thatched roofs. The roof shape suits heavy snowfall and leaves room in the loft for raising silkworms.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Japan's official island count jumped from 6,852 to 14,125 in a 2023 survey. Better maps revealed thousands of islands the earlier count had missed.
options.label: gsi.go.jp

options.text: Tripoli has a boomerang-shaped exhibition hall about 750 metres long. Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer designed it for an international fair.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bakers press their fingertips into man'ouché dough before topping it with thyme, sumac, sesame and olive oil for breakfast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Cedars of God preserve a remnant of Lebanon's ancient mountain forests. Cedar timber from this region was prized across the ancient Mediterranean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Litani makes an unusual turn. It runs south through Lebanon's inland valley, then bends west to the Mediterranean, completing a major river's entire course within the country's narrow borders.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: More than two thousand stone jars dot a plateau in Laos. Iron Age communities used them in funerary practices.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Lao khaen looks like a bundle of bamboo pipes. Each tube contains a metal reed, letting one player sound several notes together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Vat Phou, ancient planners laid out a route from mountain to plain through temples and waterworks, giving the landscape a religious axis.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia. Much of its western border is nevertheless a waterfront, formed by the Mekong River.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In kok boru, two teams on horseback compete to carry an ulak into the opposing goal. Traditionally the object in play was a goat carcass.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sulaiman-Too's five peaks rise over Osh. For more than fifteen hundred years the mountain served as both a sacred place and a landmark on the Silk Roads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kyrgyz felt carpets can be made by cutting contrasting sheets of felt together and exchanging the pieces. Two complementary patterns come out of one cut.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: About 94 per cent of Kyrgyzstan sits more than a kilometre above sea level. Even many of its low-looking valleys would count as high ground in most countries.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Before Kuwait had large desalination plants, sailing boats brought fresh water from the Shatt al-Arab. A coastal city had to import something it could see in abundance in the wrong form.
options.label: mew.gov.kw

options.text: Kuwait’s tidal islands have beaches where shorebirds nest underground. Crab-plovers excavate burrows there, gathering in colonies beside the mudflats where they forage.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The north shore of Kuwait Bay has a conspicuous ridge in an otherwise low landscape. The Jal az-Zor escarpment rises sharply behind the coastal flats.
options.label: e.gov.kw

options.text: On a bend of the Ayeyarwady at Bagan, the plain is studded with Buddhist temples and stupas built when it was an imperial capital.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Myanmar's Thingyan New Year festivities include pouring water on Buddha images. In some communities younger people also give their elders manicures and pedicures.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The ancient Pyu cities used moats, walls and waterworks in the dry zone of Myanmar. The surviving outlines are big enough to trace entire cities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Ayeyarwady runs nearly the length of Myanmar without crossing an international boundary. It fans out into a broad delta before reaching the Andaman Sea.
options.label: eol.jsc.nasa.gov

options.text: Bronze Age communities on the Mongolian steppe stood up stones engraved with stylised deer. Some of these ceremonial stones reach four metres high.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Biyelgee dances fit inside a herder's ger. Dancers can perform half-seated or cross-legged, using shoulders and hands to act out everyday work.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The carved head atop a morin khuur fiddle gives the instrument its familiar name, the horsehead fiddle. Its two strings are played with a bow.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The world's second-largest landlocked country has only two neighbours. Russia and China share Mongolia's entire land frontier between them.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Historic Maldivian mosques were built of coral carved into interlocking blocks. Builders used reef material much as mainland masons used quarried stone.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: From above, the Maldives resolve into chains of coral islands grouped in 26 natural atolls. Dry land is only a tiny part of the archipelago.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: One proposed origin for the name Maldives is a Sanskrit phrase meaning 'garland of islands', an apt description of their shape from above.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Maldives scatter the smallest land area of any Asian country across a chain of 26 natural atolls. On a map showing only dry land, almost the entire outline disappears.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Near Kuala Lumpur a mature rainforest stands on former tin-mining ground. Researchers began planting the damaged land in the 1920s.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Niah caves on Borneo, archaeologists found boat-shaped burials and a record of people using the rainforest stretching back at least 50,000 years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Songket's shimmering patterns are woven into the cloth. Weavers introduce extra gold- or silver-coloured threads between the ordinary ones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Malaysia has two large pieces with sea between them. Its eastern states are on Borneo, an island divided among three countries: Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei.
options.label: modis.gsfc.nasa.gov

options.text: Oman’s aflaj move water by gravity. Communities have used observations of the sky to divide the available irrigation time among water users.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Dhofar, frankincense starts as resin from a tree. Trees, caravan stops and seaports preserve successive stages of its old trading route.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Oman's curved khanjar dagger is made by several crafts working together. Its distinctive outline also appears on the country's emblem.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The tip of the Arabian Peninsula at the Strait of Hormuz belongs to Oman, yet is separated from the rest of Oman by the United Arab Emirates. It is the Musandam exclave.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Sediment beneath Kathmandu records an ancient lake. The Himalayan capital occupies a basin that collected mud and sand underwater before it became a valley floor.
options.label: nepjol.info

options.text: Beyond Nepal's main Himalayan crest, Upper Mustang lies in a rain shadow. A traveller can go north from wet monsoon slopes into a high, dry landscape continuous with the Tibetan Plateau.
options.label: ntb.gov.np

options.text: Nepal sets its clocks a quarter of an hour ahead of neighbouring India. Its standard meridian runs through the region of Mount Gaurishankar, giving Nepal an offset of five hours and 45 minutes from Greenwich.
options.label: giwmscdnone.gov.np

options.text: Wadi Gaza connects an arid drainage basin to a Mediterranean wetland. Its lower valley offers wet ground on the narrow route followed by migrating birds between Africa and Eurasia.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Rain sinking into the limestone along the West Bank’s central ridge can take two very different underground routes. Parts of the mountain aquifer drain west towards the coastal plain and others east towards the Jordan valley.
options.label: gov.il

options.text: At Battir, water can travel from a hillside spring to a succession of stone-walled terraces by gravity. Farmers take turns using the same flow, so the valley’s irrigation system divides water by time as well as by land.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: After an earthquake in 2013, a mud island appeared off the Pakistani port of Gwadar. Within a few years waves had worn it back below the sea.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Pakistan acquired a lake in 2010 when a landslide dammed the Hunza River. The rising water at Attabad submerged villages and a stretch of the Karakoram Highway.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Five of Earth’s fourteen independent peaks above 8,000 metres rise in or on the border of Pakistan. Four stand in the Karakoram. The fifth, Nanga Parbat, belongs to the Himalayas.
options.label: mofa.gov.pk

options.text: Sand covered the abandoned pearling port of Al Zubarah. Beneath it, archaeologists found traces of an entire Gulf town, from palaces to fishers' huts.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Among the rock carvings at Al Jassasiya are boats seen from above. Other carvings are rows of little cup-shaped hollows whose purpose is still debated.
options.label: qm.org.qa

options.text: Doha's name is usually traced to an Arabic word for a large tree. It may recall a landmark at the fishing village that preceded the capital.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Qatar is a peninsula on a peninsula. It sticks north into the Persian Gulf from the eastern side of Arabia, with just one land neighbour, Saudi Arabia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In 1256, lava travelled towards Medina from the Harrat Rahat volcanic field. The dark flow is still traceable outside the city in a country usually pictured as a sea of sand.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: Al-Ahsa in eastern Saudi Arabia has around 2.5 million date palms. Springs, wells and irrigation channels sustain one of the largest oases on Earth.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A lava flow in northern Arabia left a tunnel large enough to shelter animals for thousands of years. At Umm Jirsan, bones accumulated in passages beneath Saudi Arabia’s apparently barren volcanic surface.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: The name Pulau Ubin refers to granite. Quarries on this small Singaporean island supplied stone for structures including the causeway that links Singapore to Malaysia.
options.label: pulau-ubin.nparks.gov.sg

options.text: The Marina Barrage cut off a tidal inlet to make a freshwater reservoir in central Singapore. Its gates also let stormwater out when heavy rain threatens low-lying streets.
options.label: pub.gov.sg

options.text: Singapore makes NEWater from treated used water. Much of this exceptionally pure water goes to industries such as chipmaking, where ordinary drinking water would need more treatment.
options.label: pub.gov.sg

options.text: Damascus glassblowers give broken glass another life. They melt the scraps in brick ovens and shape the molten glass on a hollow rod.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Bosra, a Roman theatre survives inside a later fortress. The seats look out from tiers of dark basalt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In northern Syria, abandoned late-antique villages retain houses, churches and olive presses. They preserve the workings of whole farming communities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Damascus sits in an oasis. The Barada brings water down from the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, allowing a major city and its gardens to survive at the edge of the Syrian Desert.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A 660-tonne metal sphere hangs inside Taipei 101. Its motion helps steady the skyscraper when the wind makes the building sway.
options.label: www.taipei-101.com.tw

options.text: The Liwu River cut Taroko Gorge through marble as Taiwan's mountains rose. Rock that formed deep underground now makes the canyon walls.
options.label: www.taroko.gov.tw

options.text: On early European maps Taiwan often appears as Formosa. The name comes from Portuguese for 'beautiful'.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Taiwan is a mountain range still being built. The Philippine Sea and Eurasian plates converge at the island, squeezing up mountains where the two plates meet.
options.label: earthquake.usgs.gov

options.text: Sri Lanka’s Horton Plains ends at an escarpment called World’s End. A walker on relatively level montane grassland can reach a cliff edge with a drop of roughly 870 metres.
options.label: tourism.cp.gov.lk

options.text: When water recedes at the ancient Minneriya reservoir, fresh grass grows on the exposed banks. Elephants gather there in the dry season to graze.
options.label: sltda.gov.lk

options.text: Sri Lanka has two monsoons that favour different sides of the island. The central mountains intercept moist winds from the southwest, while the northeast receives much of its rain when the seasonal winds reverse.
options.label: unfccc.int

options.text: Between the Vakhsh and Panj rivers, floodwater sustains poplar forest in a dry Central Asian landscape. This riverside woodland is known as tugay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The high ranges of Eurasia meet at the Pamir Knot in eastern Tajikistan. Several peaks in its national park top 7,000 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tajik oshi palav brings rice, vegetables and meat together in one pot. Learning to cook it can involve an apprenticeship with an experienced maker.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The tallest summit in the former Soviet Union is in Tajikistan. At 7,495 metres, Ismoil Somoni Peak rises higher than any mountain in present-day Russia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Thailand’s largest lake lets you travel from fresh water through brackish water to salt water. The linked basins of Songkhla become progressively more marine towards their opening into the Gulf of Thailand.
options.label: thailand.go.th

options.text: Thailand gets frost. On Doi Inthanon, its highest mountain, cold-season mornings can leave ice crystals on the grass in a country usually associated with tropical heat.
options.label: thailandtourismdirectory.go.th

options.text: At Thailand’s Golden Triangle, three countries meet at a junction of two rivers. The Ruak separates Thailand from Myanmar before flowing into the Mekong, with Laos across the water.
options.label: tourismlaos.org

options.text: Atauro's reefs pack an exceptional variety of fish into a small space. A scientific survey counted hundreds of reef-fish species around this one Timorese island.
options.label: conservation.org

options.text: Timor-Leste's highest summit reaches nearly three kilometres above the surrounding seas. Foho Tatamailau stands in the mountainous interior of Timor.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Timor-Leste includes islands on two sides of its main territory. Atauro lies north of the capital and Jaco just off the eastern tip of Timor.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Timor-Leste lies wholly south of the equator. Its neighbours help explain why that is unusual for an Asian country: Indonesia's thousands of islands spread across both hemispheres.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Abu Dhabi's coast, seawater evaporating from low flats leaves gypsum, salt and other minerals behind. Geologists use the Arabic word sabkha for landscapes like these around the world.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In the eastern United Arab Emirates, pieces of ancient ocean floor stand above the desert. Tectonic forces pushed oceanic crust onto the Arabian margin, exposing rock that normally lies beneath the sea.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Abu Dhabi has forests that grow in seawater along the edge of the desert. Grey mangroves send breathing roots up through the mud where ordinary underground roots would struggle for oxygen.
options.label: ead.gov.ae

options.text: Merv was a succession of cities in one oasis. As rulers shifted the centre, the walls of earlier cities survived beside later ones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Turkmen dutar maker shapes a long-necked, two-stringed instrument. The same tradition encompasses building it, playing it and singing to it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Akhal-Teke horse is bred in Turkmenistan and prized for its distinctive sheen. Breeders pass knowledge of pedigrees and training down through families.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Karakum Desert occupies more than four-fifths of Turkmenistan. Most of the country's outline on a political map encloses a single desert.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Shibam, houses several storeys high rise from a walled town of mud brick. Building upwards kept the settlement compact on its floodplain.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sana'a's tall rammed-earth and brick houses have pale geometric decoration that picks out windows and walls across the old city.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Ma'rib, the ancient kingdom of Saba channelled floodwater through a great dam to irrigate fields on both sides of a desert valley.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: About 37 per cent of the plant species on Yemen's Socotra archipelago grow wild nowhere else. The islands lie off the Horn of Africa, across the water from mainland Yemen.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Archaeology at Tràng An records people adapting as the sea advanced and retreated among limestone towers. Some of today's inland cliffs once stood by the coast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Quan họ singers trade verses between groups from different villages. One group offers a song and the other answers to a matching tune.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Hồ dynasty's citadel was built in the fourteenth century. Enormous fitted stone blocks still frame its gateways.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Vietnam stretches roughly 1,650 kilometres from north to south yet narrows to about 50 kilometres across. At its waist, the sea and the Lao border are scarcely a day's cycle apart.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Uzbek askiya is a contest of wit. Speakers improvise on a shared topic, trying to outdo one another with wordplay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Samarkand's location on the Silk Roads brought artisans and ideas together. The turquoise monuments of Timur's capital stand at that old crossroads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Uzbekistan palov can turn cooking rice into work for an entire gathering. The dish is served at occasions ranging from weddings to commemorations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: From Uzbekistan, even crossing into a neighbouring country leaves you landlocked. All five of its neighbours lack an open-ocean coast, making it one of just two doubly landlocked states.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Bohol, salt makers soak coconut husks in seawater for months, burn them and boil the resulting brine in pots. The finished salt looks like an egg in a shell.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Palawan a river runs through a limestone cave and empties directly into the sea. Tides reach into its lower underground stretch.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Philippine Cordilleras, Ifugao farmers built irrigated rice terraces that follow the mountain contours. Forests above the paddies are part of the water system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: For decades schoolchildren learned that the Philippines had 7,107 islands. A new mapping effort put the figure at 7,641, without moving a single border.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Bali's subak associations coordinate irrigation through networks of water temples. Decisions made upstream affect when farmers downstream can flood their rice terraces.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Balinese dance has sacred, semi-sacred and entertainment forms. The dance appropriate inside a temple can differ from the one performed for an audience outside.
options.label: ich.unesco.org
