options.text: Lake Batur fills a volcanic crater and is regarded as a source of irrigation water. A major water temple stands beside the lake.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Over Macau's port stands the Guia Lighthouse, identified by UNESCO as China's oldest lighthouse. It shares its hill with a fortress.

options.text: Macau's map once showed Taipa and Coloane as two separate islands. Reclaimed land between them joined them together.

options.text: The University of Macau's main campus is on Hengqin Island, across the water from Macao's original territory. A special jurisdictional arrangement lets Macao administer the campus.

options.text: Green and loggerhead turtles share nesting beaches on the north coast of Cyprus. At Alagadi, tracks in the sand let researchers locate nests dug during the night.

options.text: Fresh water crosses the Mediterranean from Turkey to northern Cyprus inside a pipe. Along the deep-water stretch the pipe hangs suspended beneath the surface rather than resting on the seabed.

options.text: Donkeys roam free on the Karpaz Peninsula. Descendants of working animals now graze the long finger of land pointing northeast from Cyprus.

options.text: The Kudaro caves preserve bones of Ice Age big cats. What is now a mountain cave in South Ossetia once lay within the range of animals known mainly from fossils.

options.text: The high country around Lake Keli is volcanic. Lava flows built up a plateau on the southern flank of the Caucasus, within a range better known for mountains raised by collision.

options.text: Lake Ertso in South Ossetia can disappear into the ground. It occupies a karst basin where underground drainage can empty the lake and leave a hollow until the water returns.

options.text: Mount Bromo rises out of a broad volcanic caldera with a floor known as the Sea of Sand. The “sea” is dry volcanic material surrounded by steep crater walls.
options.label: indonesia.travel

options.text: Semeru is the highest volcano on Java. Its summit rises more than 3,600 metres above a tropical island crossed by a chain of other volcanoes.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: The ground at Sangiran formed in changing environments. Its exposed layers preserve a sequence from marine deposits to land deposits bearing early human remains.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The world's most populous island is Java. At night a ribbon of cities lights up the length of an island small enough to disappear on some world maps.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: A Sumatran forest can produce a single flower about a metre across. Rafflesia spends most of its life hidden inside a host vine before its enormous blossom emerges.
options.label: powo.science.kew.org

options.text: Sumatra's rainforests shelter elephants, tigers, rhinoceroses and orangutans on the same island. All four have distinct Sumatran populations.

options.text: Indonesia's highest volcano is on Sumatra. Mount Kerinci rises about 3,800 metres amid the forest of Kerinci Seblat National Park.

options.text: A British sovereign base on Cyprus contains a wetland of international importance. Akrotiri's salt lake and marshes share the peninsula with the military base.
options.label: www.ramsar.org

options.text: Greater flamingos feed in the wetland at Akrotiri. The suitability of the lake for the birds changes as water levels fluctuate.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Dhekelia is a British territory with pieces of the Republic of Cyprus inside it. The villages of Ormideia and Xylotymbou are enclaves within the base area's outline.

options.text: On Jeju, people welcome the wind goddess Yeongdeung with rites for calm seas and a good catch, then mark her departure with a farewell ceremony.

options.text: At Sindou, erosion has left a skyline of sandstone needles rising above the savanna. The towers are the surviving pieces of a once continuous mass of rock.

options.text: The Black Volta has a floodplain lake known as the Mare aux Hippopotames. In the dry country of western Burkina Faso its lake and marshes sustain a resident population of hippos.

options.text: Among Cameroon's Bamoun, the Nguon includes a public trial of the king's governance. Ritual chiefs present criticisms collected from the community.

options.text: In the Sawa Ngondo ceremony, a priest dives from a sacred canoe into the Wouri River. People gather on the banks to await the water oracle's message.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Dja River curves around nearly the whole Dja forest reserve. The water forms a natural boundary for a rainforest inhabited by gorillas and chimpanzees.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Cameroon sits at the bend in Africa's Atlantic coastline. Here the east–west coast of West Africa turns south, earning the country the nickname 'the hinge of Africa'.

options.text: Burundi's royal drummers combine synchronised beats with leaps, songs and heroic poetry. A group arranges its drums around a central drum.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Rain falling in Burundi can head for opposite sides of Africa. The country straddles the watershed between the Nile and Congo systems.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The borders of the precolonial kingdom of Burundi in the nineteenth century already resembled those of the modern country.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Landlocked Burundi has an international shipping port. Vessels leaving Bujumbura can travel hundreds of kilometres south along Lake Tanganyika towards Zambia.

options.text: The cape in Cabo Verde's name is not on the islands. It is a peninsula on the Senegalese mainland, hundreds of kilometres to the east.

options.text: In Cabo Verde's morna songs, departure, separation and the longing to return are recurring subjects in music shaped by island life.

options.text: The islands of Cabo Verde belong to Macaronesia along with the Azores, Madeira and Canaries. Of those four Atlantic archipelagos, Cabo Verde alone forms an independent country.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: São Tomé and Príncipe are mountaintops in the Gulf of Guinea. They belong to a chain of volcanoes rising out of the Atlantic.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: São Tomé's old agricultural estates are known as roças. Cocoa and coffee plantations became a defining feature of the island's inhabited landscape.

options.text: The two islands are named for very different figures. São Tomé honours Saint Thomas, while Príncipe's original name referred to a Portuguese prince.

options.text: Africa's second-smallest country consists chiefly of two islands named São Tomé and Príncipe. Only Seychelles has less land among Africa's independent states.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A rainforest at the southwestern tip of the country continues across two borders. The three adjoining national parks of the Sangha Trinational lie in Cameroon, the Central African Republic and the Republic of the Congo.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In the Sahara, the Ounianga lakes include both fresh and intensely salty water. Underground supplies keep them from vanishing in the desert heat.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wind and water carved arches and canyons into the Ennedi sandstone. Some deep canyons hold water year-round in the middle of the Sahara.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Chad used to be part of an enormous inland sea. The animals of the wetter Sahara included hippos, giraffes and elephants.

options.text: Africa's largest landlocked country takes its name from a lake. Chad stretches from the shrinking waters on its western frontier far north into the Sahara.

options.text: The equator misses every piece of dry land in Equatorial Guinea. Its mainland lies north of the line, while the island of Annobón lies south of it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Bioko you can climb from lowland rainforest into a very different mountain forest on the same small island. Its slopes shelter distinctive island primates.

options.text: Equatorial Guinea's mainland and Bioko are separate enough that a voyage from one to the other passes the coast of another country, Cameroon.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Lake Turkana has volcanic islands inside a desert lake. Central Island and South Island are national parks surrounded by water in one of Kenya's driest regions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Gedi was a Swahili trading town on Kenya's coast. Its stone ruins now stand in forest, where archaeological finds reveal connections across the Indian Ocean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kenya spans two hemispheres, yet its main ocean port, Mombasa, is well south of the equator. The equator crosses the country's interior on its way to Somalia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: There are glaciers almost on the equator in Kenya. Mount Kenya rises high enough for ice to survive only a few kilometres south of the line separating the hemispheres.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Coelacanths shelter together in underwater volcanic caves off Grande Comore by day. After dark they leave the caves to hunt along the island’s steep submarine slopes.
options.label: frontiersin.org

options.text: The entire wild range of Livingstone’s fruit bat fits on two Comorian islands, Anjouan and Mohéli. Even Grande Comore, the biggest island in the country, falls outside it.
options.label: batcon.org

options.text: Anjouan stores drinking water in a volcano. Lake Dzialandzé occupies a crater high on the island and supplies freshwater to communities below.
options.label: ramsar.org

options.text: On some earthen mosques in northern Côte d'Ivoire, the projecting buttresses are topped with pottery or ostrich eggs.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Attiéké looks rather like couscous, but its grains start as cassava. The makers ferment and granulate the root before steaming it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Zaouli performances among the Guro, a carved mask and costume turn the dancer into a character. Percussion drives remarkably intricate footwork.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Comoé River carries a strip of forest far into the Ivorian savanna. Riverbanks let species associated with more humid country reach much farther north than the surrounding grassland would suggest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The striped-legged okapi lives in the forests of the Congo Basin. The Ituri reserve protects part of the range of this elusive giraffe relative.

options.text: Salonga protects a vast tract of rainforest reached chiefly by water. Among its inhabitants is the bonobo, an ape found only in this country.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Virunga encompasses volcanoes, mountain gorilla habitat and the snowy Rwenzori highlands within the same national park.

options.text: Africa's second-largest country reaches the Atlantic through a tiny opening. Almost the whole outline of the DR Congo lies inland, while a narrow corridor follows the lower Congo River to the sea.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Assal sits below sea level. Its shore is the lowest exposed land in Africa.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Ships sailing from the Indian Ocean to Suez pass Djibouti at the entrance to the Red Sea. A small stretch of coastline sits beside an intercontinental sea route.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Three great rifts converge in the Afar region around Djibouti. The Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African Rift mark three different directions in which the crust is pulling apart.

options.text: Hippos on Guinea-Bissau's Bijagós islands swim in salt water. Tidal channels separate islands used by an animal usually associated with freshwater rivers and lakes.

options.label: unora.unior.it

options.text: At Lalibela, churches were excavated down into rock. Some stand free inside trenches, with their roofs near the level where a builder above ground would normally start.

options.text: Leatherback turtles return to Gabon's Atlantic beaches to lay eggs. A forested country on the equator contains some of this ocean traveller's most important nesting shores.

options.text: The lowest point in Lesotho is about 1,400 metres above the sea. No other country's lowest point is that high.

options.text: Liberia's capital commemorates an American president. Monrovia was named for James Monroe.

options.text: In Madagascar's dry country, rain has carved limestone into the needle-like ridges called tsingy. The maze shelters wildlife isolated between the rocks.

options.text: Zafimaniry craftspeople use wood for houses, furniture and intricately carved surfaces. Timber joints hold the traditional homes together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Malagasy kabary speakers weave proverbs, riddles and wordplay into public speeches. Their performance can turn a family occasion into an exercise in poetry.

options.text: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island. Its long isolation means roughly nine in ten of its plant and animal species occur nowhere else.

options.text: Farmers and hunter-gatherers both left paintings at Chongoni. The granite hills of central Malawi preserve rock art from people who used the same landscape in different ways.

options.text: Malawi reaches its lowest elevation where the Shire meets Mozambique. That point is over 400 metres below the surface of the great lake that feeds the river.

options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A population of elephants survives on the edge of the Sahara in Mali. The Gourma herd follows a great seasonal circuit between waterholes, reaching different parts of the landscape as they dry out.
options.label: wild.org

options.text: The Senegal River begins in Mali. At Bafoulabé, the Bafing and Bakoye join to form a river named for a country it has yet to reach.
options.label: omvs.org

options.text: Mali has seven neighbours, and five have their own seacoasts. From this landlocked country a traveller can enter a neighbour facing the Mediterranean, or choose among four facing the Atlantic.
options.label: ecowap.ecowas.int

options.text: At Banc d'Arguin the Sahara meets extensive tidal flats. Birds that breed as far away as northern Eurasia spend the winter feeding there.

options.text: Chinguetti and three other desert towns grew up to shelter caravans. Their compact streets also supported scholars and religious schools.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Mauritanian mahadra is a community school that can travel with its teachers and students, a form of education suited to nomadic life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Eye of the Sahara looks like an enormous impact crater from space. Its rings in Mauritania are layers of an eroded geological dome.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Mauritius has crystals billions of years older than the island itself. Zircons carried up in its volcanic rock are evidence of ancient continental crust beneath the young island.

options.text: Mauritius and Île aux Aigrettes face each other across less than a kilometre of water, yet one is volcanic and the other is built of coral limestone.
options.label: mauritian-wildlife.org

options.text: The whole world population of Mauritius kestrels fell to four known birds in 1974. One remaining wild breeding pair helped give the island species a way back.
options.label: mauritian-wildlife.org

options.text: Producing argan oil involves cracking the hard nut, grinding the kernels and working the paste to release the oil. The tree grows in Morocco's southwest.

options.text: In Marrakesh, storytellers, musicians and other performers make Jemaa el-Fna square into an open-air venue whose programme changes through the day.

options.text: At Aït-Ben-Haddou, a group of earthen houses sits inside defensive walls. The fortified settlement stood along a caravan route between the Sahara and Marrakesh.

options.text: North Africa's highest summit is in Morocco. At 4,167 metres, Toubkal in the High Atlas can carry snow surprisingly close to the Sahara.

options.text: West African giraffes survived around Kouré alongside farms and villages. The last remnant of this giraffe population lived outside a national park, browsing trees in a working landscape.

options.text: At Bilma in the Sahara, people make salt using water. Brine evaporates in shallow pans and the salt can be carried across the surrounding sand sea.

options.text: The Cross River gorilla’s entire range straddles a short stretch of the Nigeria–Cameroon border. Its scattered groups survive on forested highlands on both sides of the frontier.

options.text: The Niger ends in a forest that grows in salt water. Its many outlets spread into the largest mangrove system in Africa before they enter the Gulf of Guinea.

options.text: At Yankari in Nigeria, Wikki Warm Spring feeds a clear pool at about 31°C. Water flowing from the rock keeps the pool warm through the seasons.

options.text: Odzala-Kokoua's rainforest opens into swampy clearings known as bais. They draw animals out from under the canopy, including forest elephants.

options.text: Brazzaville and Kinshasa, capitals of two separate countries, face each other across the Congo River.

options.text: The centres of Congolese rumba face one another across a river. Musicians in Brazzaville and Kinshasa developed a shared urban dance tradition in two different countries.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The Republic of the Congo and its neighbour share the world's largest tropical peatland complex. Beneath the Cuvette Centrale's swamp forest, waterlogged ground has stored carbon for thousands of years.

options.text: Lake Kivu once drained north. Volcanic activity blocked that route, and today water leaves Rwanda’s western shore southward by the Ruzizi, bound for Lake Tanganyika.

options.text: Rwanda’s mountain gorillas can change countries without leaving their forest. The Virunga habitat is shared with Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

options.text: Ceebu jën, rice and fish cooked with vegetables, is closely associated with Saint-Louis. Its preparation and the way diners share the platter are both part of the tradition.

options.text: Ancient burial grounds in Senegal and The Gambia are marked with circles of upright laterite stones cut from nearby quarries.

options.text: The Djoudj wetlands lie just south of the Sahara. For birds flying across the desert, the Senegal River delta offers a first major place to feed and rest.

options.text: The westernmost point of mainland Africa is in Dakar. Senegal's Cap-Vert peninsula projects farther into the Atlantic than the rest of the continent's mainland coast.

options.text: Aldabra's remote coral atoll supports an enormous wild population of giant tortoises. Much of the land surrounding its lagoon sits only a little above the tide.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Enslaved Africans in Seychelles once danced moutya at night away from plantation houses. Performers warm the goatskin drum near a fire before playing.

options.text: In the Gola forest and on Tiwai Island, pygmy hippos share the Upper Guinean forest region with forest elephants and white-necked rockfowl.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sierra Leone's name comes from Portuguese for 'Lion Mountains'. Sailors applied it to the mountains rising beside what is now Freetown.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Parts of Sierra Leone's Atlantic coast receive almost five metres of rain a year. Its mountainous shore is among the wettest stretches of coastal West Africa.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: South Africa completely surrounds a country whose lowest ground is above 1,000 metres. Every overland trip into or out of the mountain kingdom of Lesotho crosses South Africa.

options.text: South Africa’s sardine run can lead the fish into a trap. Research traced many of the migrants to cooler Atlantic waters, even though their spectacular journey takes them up the warmer Indian Ocean coast.
