options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Red Sea has just one atoll, according to UNESCO. Sanganeb rises from deep water about 25 kilometres off Sudan, a ring of coral surrounding a lagoon.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: A vanished river once joined the Nile from the west across what is now the Sahara. Its dry course, Wadi Howar, still crosses northern Sudan.
options.label: uni-koeln.de

options.text: Sail north from Sudan’s Lake Nubia and you can enter Egypt’s Lake Nasser without leaving the reservoir. The names belong to different national stretches of the water behind the Aswan High Dam.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Eswatini almost fits inside South Africa's outline. Only along its eastern side does its border meet a second country, Mozambique.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The government and the monarchy have different seats. Mbabane is the administrative capital, while the royal and legislative centre is at Lobamba.
options.label: sadc.int

options.text: Eswatini's elevation ranges from about 21 metres on the Great Usutu River to more than 1,800 at Emlembe. The ocean is outside the country, but part of its river valley is barely above sea level.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Cross Eswatini from west to east and the country steps down from the Highveld through the Middleveld into the Lowveld, then rises again in the Lubombo hills on the Mozambique border.
options.label: ewade.co.sz

options.text: At Ngorongoro you can descend into a huge volcanic caldera and see grazing herds on its floor. Nearby Olduvai preserves evidence of early humans.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The great Serengeti migration follows changing access to water and grass. Wildebeest, zebras and gazelles move across the plains with predators following.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Kondoa rock shelters, painted figures have survived under natural overhangs. Some of the sites still have ritual uses for nearby communities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Africa's highest point is close to the equator in Tanzania. Kilimanjaro rises nearly 5,900 metres above sea level without belonging to a long chain of comparable summits.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Koutammakou, Batammariba families build earthen tower houses called takienta. The houses give this part of northern Togo its distinctive skyline.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Among the Guin of southern Togo, taking a sacred stone marks the new year. The rite belongs to a cycle of ceremonies that lasts several months.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The country takes its name from a settlement on Lake Togo. The name likely combines Ewe words for water and shore.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Togo has a short Atlantic frontage but stretches hundreds of kilometres inland. Follow its long axis north and a narrow coastal country becomes a land of dry savannas.
options.label: documents.un.org

options.text: In the Kerkennah Islands, fishers plant palm fronds in the seabed. The outgoing tide helps guide fish along these barriers into chambers and traps.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Roman amphitheatre at El Jem rises over a small Tunisian town. Its huge freestanding oval remains one of the clearest traces of Roman Africa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Making harissa traditionally begins with drying red peppers in the sun. Families grind them with seasonings to make the paste.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mainland Africa reaches farther north in Tunisia than in any other country. The northern tip is near Bizerte, across the Mediterranean from Europe.
options.label: comesa.int

options.text: At Murchison Falls an entire branch of the Nile squeezes through a gap only about seven metres wide before plunging into the gorge below.
options.label: ugandawildlife.org

options.text: Floating islands can dam the Nile in Uganda. Mats of papyrus and other vegetation have blocked the outlet of shallow Lake Kyoga, backing water up across its shores.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Uganda’s Bwindi forest shelters one of just two surviving populations of mountain gorillas. It is physically separated from the other population on the Virunga volcanoes.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Fish survive in permanent pools in the desert at Sebkhat Imlili in Western Sahara. The isolated pools preserve a remnant of a much wetter Saharan landscape.
options.label: ramsar.org

options.text: Mediterranean monk seals have an Atlantic stronghold. They breed in sea caves on the Cabo Blanco peninsula on the Western Saharan and Mauritanian coast.
options.label: marinemammalhabitat.org

options.text: Dust from Western Sahara can cross the ocean to the Canary Islands. Satellites have caught plumes broad enough to hide much of the archipelago in a single event.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: One direct road between Zambia’s Copperbelt and Luapula Province crosses another country twice. The Congo Pedicle, a tongue of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sticks into Zambia between them.
options.label: parliament.gov.zm

options.text: Each rainy season millions of straw-coloured fruit bats converge on one patch of swamp forest in Zambia’s Kasanka National Park, then disperse again as the fruit supply changes.
options.label: zambia.travel

options.text: Four countries draw close at Kazungula, yet Zambia and Botswana share a short border of their own. The bridge across the Zambezi links the pair between Namibia and Zimbabwe.
options.label: afdb.org

options.text: A narrow stripe of rock runs for more than 500 kilometres across Zimbabwe. Called the Great Dyke, it formed when magma intruded into older rock and is visible from orbit.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Runde River runs beneath a wall of red sandstone at Chilojo. Erosion has exposed layered cliffs above a floodplain where elephants can walk across the river in the dry season.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Zimbabwe’s Chimanimani Mountains continue into Mozambique. Their quartzite ridges form an island of habitat for plants whose entire known ranges fit inside this one cross-border mountain chain.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: On La Gomera, Silbo Gomero carries spoken Spanish as whistles. A conversation can travel across ravines that would make a visit on foot a long journey.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The laurel forest at Garajonay depends on moisture carried in by sea fog. It survives high on La Gomera above much drier slopes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tenerife's Mount Teide rises from the ocean floor. Measured from that submerged base, the volcanic edifice is much taller than its height above sea level.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some old European maps counted longitude from the Canary Islands. The Ferro meridian took its name from El Hierro, once treated as the western edge of the known world.
options.label: epsg.io

options.text: Somali frankincense is harvested by tapping Boswellia trees. Different species yield distinct resins that traders recognise by name.
options.label: www.fao.org

options.text: Summer winds off Somalia can bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the sunlit surface. The monsoon helps feed ocean life as well as bringing rain to land.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Medieval trading towns on the Somali coast linked the Horn to Arabia and Persia. The sea was a trade route between communities on opposite shores.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Somalia has the longest coastline of any mainland African country. Its shore turns the corner from the Gulf of Aden onto the Indian Ocean at the Horn of Africa.
options.label: nbs.gov.so

options.text: During ice ages you could walk from mainland Africa to Unguja, Zanzibar’s largest island. The deeper channel around nearby Pemba kept it an island even as sea level fell.
options.label: frontiersin.org

options.text: The Pemba flying fox is found naturally on just one island of the Zanzibar archipelago. The narrow channel to mainland Tanzania is already beyond its native range.
options.label: cambridge.org

options.text: A forest on Zanzibar’s Chumbe Island grows on an old coral reef. The porous rock holds so little groundwater that the trees survive largely on the rain that reaches them directly.
options.label: chumbeisland.com

options.text: A sacred wooden xylophone in Guinea, the Sosso-Bala, is tied to the story of the Mali Empire. Its music accompanies the epic of Sunjata.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Mount Nimba, steep slopes and high grasslands rise above the surrounding forests. The mountain shelters an unusual live-bearing toad.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Niger begins in Guinea quite close to the Atlantic. From there it takes a long detour into the West African interior before reaching the ocean.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Guinea's highlands act as West Africa's water tower. Rivers feeding the Niger, Senegal and Gambia systems leave the country in different directions.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: From space, Libya’s Al Khufrah oasis looks covered in green coins. Rotating irrigation arms grow circular fields using ancient groundwater under one of the driest parts of the Sahara.
options.label: eol.jsc.nasa.gov

options.text: Lakes survive between the dunes of Libya’s Ubari Sand Sea. Some are saltier than the sea even though there is no ocean anywhere near them.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: In eastern Libya the scar of an asteroid impact appears as a set of concentric rings. At the BP impact structure erosion has exposed the deformed rock beneath the original crater floor.
options.label: geokniga.org

options.text: A frankincense tree formally described in 2019 was already familiar to local resin harvesters. Its entire known range at the time was a small area around Ceel Afweyn in Somaliland.
options.label: biotaxa.org

options.text: In Somaliland’s Golis Mountains, coastal mist supplies water to high forests above an arid plain. Facing the Gulf of Aden can make a mountainside wetter even when little rain falls.
options.label: faoswalim.org

options.text: Coral islands off Zeila provide nesting ground for seabirds just offshore from Somaliland’s dry mainland. The islands and their surrounding reefs form the Saad ad-Din archipelago.
options.label: rris.biopama.org

options.text: South Sudan’s capital sits near a break in the navigable Nile. Boats can travel north from Juba, while upstream a stretch of rapids towards Nimule interrupts the river route to Uganda.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: South Sudan rises from the flat Nile basin to a summit above 3,000 metres. Mount Kinyeti in the Imatong Mountains reaches an entirely different climate from the hot plains below.
options.label: mofaic.gov.ss

options.text: Parts of South Sudan have ground that moves with the seasons. The heavy clay known as black cotton soil opens deep cracks as it dries, then swells and can make roads impassable when the rains return.
options.label: assets.publishing.service.gov.uk

options.text: Beginning in 2018, earthquake swarms off Mayotte led scientists to a newly formed volcano deep beneath the Indian Ocean.
options.label: www.brgm.fr

options.text: Mayotte's waters attract five species of sea turtle. Green and hawksbill turtles use the island's reefs, seagrass beds and nesting beaches.
options.label: ofb.gouv.fr

options.text: Mayotte's marine park protects an entire sequence of habitats. Mangroves line the shore, seagrass grows in the lagoon, and coral reefs stand farther out.
options.label: ofb.gouv.fr

options.text: Parts of Mayotte's lagoon are protected by two coral barriers. This uncommon double reef puts another line of shelter between the island and the open Indian Ocean.
options.label: ofb.gouv.fr

options.text: Three immense natural amphitheatres, or cirques, cut deep into Réunion's volcanic interior. Steep enclosing walls separate valleys that look close on a map.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Enslaved Malagasy and African people helped create Réunion's maloya. The music combines singing, percussion and dance and has also served as a voice of protest.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Piton de la Fournaise is an active shield volcano. Some eruptions have sent lava down Réunion's slopes all the way to the Indian Ocean.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: Réunion holds the World Meteorological Organization's 24-hour rainfall record. At Foc-Foc, 1,825 millimetres fell in a single day during a tropical cyclone in 1966.
options.label: wmo.int

options.text: At Potosí, silver mining high in the Andes depended on artificial lakes. Aqueducts carried their water to the mills that crushed ore from Cerro Rico.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The centrepiece of Samaipata is an enormous outcrop transformed by carving. The ceremonial space was cut into the hill itself.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kallawaya healers travelled through different Andean ecological zones to learn and practise their craft. Their knowledge of plants drew on environments far beyond a single valley.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The world's largest salt flat lies high in the Andes of landlocked Bolivia. When shallow water covers the Salar de Uyuni, thousands of square kilometres turn into a mirror.
options.label: eol.jsc.nasa.gov

options.text: Chinchorro fishing communities on the Atacama coast intentionally mummified their dead thousands of years before the celebrated Egyptian royal mummies.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Andean mining town of Sewell was so steep that stairs formed its main routes. Its copper miners lived in a town largely without streets for vehicles.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Chile's old nitrate works supplied fertiliser made from desert deposits. Humberstone and Santa Laura preserve whole industrial communities in one of Earth's driest regions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The highest active volcano on Earth, Ojos del Salado, rises on Chile's border with Argentina. Its summit is nearly 6,900 metres up, on the edge of the Atacama Desert.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Beside Guyana’s Kaieteur Falls, a frog can spend its whole life in a plant. The golden rocket frog lays eggs on bromeliad leaves, and its tadpoles grow in the rainwater trapped between them.
options.label: protectedareastrust.org.gy

options.text: Four species of sea turtle nest along Guyana’s Shell Beach. The beach earns its name from its building material, great stretches of broken shells deposited along the Atlantic shore.
options.label: pac.gov.gy

options.text: In the flooded savannas of the Rupununi, one of the largest freshwater fish gives away its position by breathing. The arapaima must surface for air, which allows communities to count fish in an otherwise opaque lake.
options.label: rupununi.org

options.text: Follow the Paraná along Paraguay’s eastern and southern borders and you pass two giant power plants. Paraguay shares Itaipú with Brazil and Yacyretá with Argentina, on the very same river.
options.label: un.org

options.text: Landlocked Paraguay operates a large merchant river fleet. Barges can take its exports to Atlantic ports along the Paraguay and Paraná rivers without ever putting the cargo on a road.
options.label: unctad.org

options.text: In Paraguay’s dry Chaco, bottle trees store water in swollen trunks. Their bulging outlines are visible above scrubland that goes for months with little rain.
options.label: paraguay.wcs.org

options.text: In the forest beside the Suriname River, Jodensavanne preserves a seventeenth-century Jewish settlement with a synagogue, cemeteries and boat landings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Paramaribo's historic centre translates European building plans into a local material. Much of this tropical capital's old architecture is made of wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects headwaters and mountains deep in the rainforest. Huge smooth granite domes rise abruptly above the canopy.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Suriname is the smallest independent country in South America. Neighbouring French Guiana is smaller on the map but is part of France.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Near Atlántida, engineer Eladio Dieste made a church roof and walls undulate like waves. The material behind the curves is reinforced brick.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fray Bentos became a familiar name on European tins because a factory on the Uruguay River turned cattle from the surrounding grasslands into meat extract and corned beef.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Montevideo's candombe, different-sized drums play interlocking parts. Marching drummers connect the tradition to particular streets and neighbourhoods.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Uruguay's highest natural point barely clears 500 metres. Across a continent famous for the Andes, this country's high point is a low, rounded hill.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A satellite survey found Earth’s greatest concentration of lightning over Venezuela’s Lake Maracaibo. Winds off the lake and surrounding mountains feed thunderstorms in much the same place night after night.
options.label: earthdata.nasa.gov

options.text: Venezuela became the first Andean country to lose its last glacier. Ice remained below Pico Humboldt in 2024, but the patch had shrunk too much to flow under its own weight.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: At the mouth of the Orinoco, Atlantic tides reach into a tropical forest. The river breaks into a web of channels through which both freshwater and tidal water travel.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: France’s largest wetland lies in South America. The marshes of Kaw in French Guiana also shelter one of the continent’s last stable populations of black caiman.
options.label: guyane.developpement-durable.gouv.fr

options.text: You can spend euros on the South American mainland without exchanging them for local currency. French Guiana uses the same legal tender as metropolitan France.
options.label: ecb.europa.eu

options.text: French Guiana’s Îles du Salut lie under a flight path from the Guiana Space Centre. Islands used as a penal colony have to be evacuated for certain rocket launches.
options.label: cnes.fr

options.text: The Falklands have rivers made of boulders. These stone runs are long bands of quartzite blocks left by Ice Age conditions, some stretching for kilometres.
options.label: falklands.gov.fk

options.text: Five kinds of penguin breed in the Falklands, including king, gentoo and southern rockhopper. They share the islands but use different nesting places.
options.label: falklands.gov.fk

options.text: Darwin met the Falklands' native wolf, the warrah, and predicted its disappearance. Within decades of his visit the animal was extinct.
options.label: falklands-museum.com

options.text: The Falklands' jagged coasts include drowned valleys. Falkland Sound, the long channel down the middle of the archipelago, separates East Falkland from West Falkland.
options.label: falklands.gov.fk

options.text: A surveying assumption left Minnesota with a piece reachable by road only through Canada. A treaty told surveyors to draw a line west from Lake of the Woods to the Mississippi, but the river was too far south.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Count longitude east or west from Greenwich and Alaska is both the easternmost and westernmost US state. Its Aleutian Islands cross the 180th meridian.
options.label: alaska.gov

options.text: There is exactly one point in the United States where four states meet. At Four Corners, a step can take you between Arizona, Utah, Colorado and New Mexico.
options.label: navajonationparks.org

options.text: Puerto Rico and San Juan effectively traded names. San Juan originally named the island, while Puerto Rico, or 'rich port', referred to its harbour settlement.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Vieques, tiny organisms light up when the water around them moves. At night, a paddle can leave a glowing trail through Mosquito Bay.
options.label: www.discoverpuertorico.com

options.text: The Arecibo telescope's giant dish sat in a natural sinkhole. Puerto Rico's limestone landscape provided the bowl for an instrument that listened to space.
options.label: www.nsf.gov

options.text: Just north of Puerto Rico the ocean floor plunges deeper than anywhere else in the Atlantic. The Puerto Rico Trench reaches more than eight kilometres below the surface.
options.label: repository.library.noaa.gov

options.text: In San Pedro de Macorís, descendants of English-speaking Caribbean migrants developed Cocolo dance drama. The performances mix African-derived dance with plots from European traditions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Dominican merengue is danced in couples. The accordion, drum and scraped güira give a typical ensemble its distinctive sound.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Santo Domingo's colonial city laid out a grid that Spanish planners subsequently used as a model elsewhere in the Americas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Caribbean's highest summit and lowest exposed ground are both in the Dominican Republic. Pico Duarte rises over three kilometres high, while Lake Enriquillo's shore lies below sea level.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Haitians serve joumou, a squash soup, on Independence Day. A dish associated with colonial exclusion became a meal shared to mark freedom.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The mountaintop Citadelle was built in the years following Haitian independence. Its commanding position was meant to defend the new country.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Haiti's compas grew into a dance music heard far beyond the country. Musicians of the Haitian diaspora helped carry it around the Caribbean and overseas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Haiti occupies roughly the western third of Hispaniola. Its neighbour on the very same island, the Dominican Republic, covers about twice as much land.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Dunn’s River Falls, the waterfall builds its own staircase. Calcium carbonate comes out of the flowing water and adds fresh travertine to the ledges above the Caribbean.
options.label: dunnsriverfallsja.com

options.text: Where Jamaica’s Martha Brae River meets the sea, the lagoon can light up around a moving boat. Disturbing the water triggers flashes from microscopic organisms.
options.label: jis.gov.jm

options.text: Jamaica’s Black River runs through an extensive peat wetland. Organic matter stains the water so dark that the river takes its name from what looks like its colour.
options.label: nepa.gov.jm

options.text: In 1964 an island of mud rose from the sea off Trinidad. An offshore mud volcano pushed it above the surface near Chatham, where the same fold in the rock continues beneath the land.
options.label: pubs.geoscienceworld.org

options.text: Tobago set aside the forest along its Main Ridge in 1776 to protect rainfall and water supplies. The reserve still follows the mountain backbone whose streams feed the rest of the island.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Trinidad has a fruit-eating bird that navigates dark caves by echo. Oilbirds roost underground by day, then leave after dark to collect fruit in the forest.
options.label: biodiversity.gov.tt

options.text: La Soufrière on Basse-Terre is an active volcano with a summit dome. Steam vents are a reminder that its plumbing is still hot.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: In Guadeloupean gwoka, singers, dancers and drummers face one another in a circle. The lead drummer responds to the dancer's movements.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The Îlets Pigeon shelter reefs just off Guadeloupe's leeward coast. The national park extends underwater around these tiny islands.
options.label: www.guadeloupe-parcnational.fr

options.text: Guadeloupe's two main islands look like butterfly wings, but their rocks are quite different. Mountainous Basse-Terre is volcanic, while much flatter Grande-Terre has a limestone surface.
options.label: culture.gouv.fr

options.text: The pale turquoise around the Bahama Banks marks water shallow enough for sunlight to reach pale carbonate sand. Narrow deep channels stand out in dark blue.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: At Junkanoo, groups parade in costumes built and decorated by hand. Cowbells, drums and whistles carry the rhythm through the streets.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Andros, openings called blue holes lead into flooded limestone caves. Some lie inland, so you can encounter one well away from the coast.
options.label: www.bahamas.com

options.text: The Tongue of the Ocean is a deep submarine canyon between Bahamian banks. Its sheer sides put deep blue ocean water almost beside pale, sunlit reef flats.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: An underground river can cross from Belize into Guatemala. The Chiquibul Cave System, the largest known in Central America, extends beneath the international border.
options.label: caves.org

options.text: Belize is the only country on the Central American isthmus with no Pacific coast. Its entire seaboard faces the Caribbean.
options.label: dgff2021.unctad.org

options.text: The world’s first jaguar preserve was established in Belize. It protects the forested Cockscomb Basin, where mountains collect the water that flows out through the jaguars’ habitat.
options.label: rris.biopama.org

options.text: In the Diquís Delta, pre-Columbian craftspeople carved large stone spheres of remarkable precision. Some still mark the approaches to former settlements.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Costa Rica's painted oxcarts once hauled coffee to the Pacific. Distinct designs grew up in different regions, making some carts recognisable by their decoration.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Guanacaste protects a route from Pacific shore through tropical dry forest into cloud forest. Animals can move between sharply different climates within one conservation area.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: From the top of Cerro Chirripó on an exceptionally clear day it is possible to see both the Pacific and the Caribbean. Costa Rica's highest summit stands between them.
options.label: sinac.go.cr

options.text: Volcanic ash buried the farming community at Joya de Cerén. It preserved houses and domestic objects that show how ordinary families lived.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: El Salvador is the one Central American country whose entire seacoast faces the Pacific. It has no Caribbean shore.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Panchimalco, the Confraternity of Flowers and Palms decorates palm fronds with flowers for a procession. Preparing them brings generations of neighbours together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: El Salvador is the smallest country on mainland Central America. All of its coastline fits along the Pacific between Guatemala and the Gulf of Fonseca.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez, communities build giant kites for the season of the dead. Elaborate pictures are assembled from coloured paper.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Maya city of Tikal, tall temples rise through forest occupied by howler monkeys. The national park protects the ruins and their rainforest together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Quiriguá, Maya sculptors carved immense stone stelae. Their inscriptions record dates and dynastic events in the city's own words.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The highest mountain in Central America is a volcano in Guatemala. Tajumulco reaches about 4,220 metres near the Mexican border.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Copán, Maya builders turned a staircase into a written monument. Carved glyphs run over the steps of its Hieroglyphic Stairway.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Río Plátano reserve follows a river from mountains to the Caribbean. Indigenous communities live within the protected forest landscape.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Honduras has two very unequal coasts. Its long Caribbean frontage contrasts with a short reach of Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Bay Islands of Honduras belong to a reef that crosses four countries. From Roatán the Mesoamerican Reef system continues along Guatemala, Belize and Mexico.
options.label: roatanmarinepark.org

options.text: When León moved in the seventeenth century, the old town stayed behind. The ruins of León Viejo preserve the layout of an early Spanish colonial settlement.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In El Güegüense, a wily merchant outtalks colonial authorities. Masks, dance and satire keep the story alive in Nicaragua.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: León Cathedral's apparently simple outer walls hide a more elaborate interior. Its design reflects the need for a massive building to survive local earthquakes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Central America's largest country also contains its largest lake. Lake Nicaragua takes up a sizeable part of the narrow strip separating the two American continents.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: One gap breaks the Pan-American Highway between North and South America. At the Darién, the road gives way to rainforest and wetlands on the Panama–Colombia border.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Filling the Panama Canal turned a hilltop into an island. Barro Colorado’s forest was cut off from neighbouring forest by Gatún Lake, creating a century-long experiment in island ecology.
options.label: striresearch.si.edu

options.text: The rise of the Isthmus of Panama closed a passage for marine animals and opened one for land animals. Mammals could walk between the Americas while Caribbean and Pacific sea life began evolving apart.
options.label: stri.si.edu

options.text: Steam and bubbling water fill Dominica's Boiling Lake. It occupies a flooded volcanic vent in Morne Trois Pitons National Park.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Kalinago Territory, craftspeople preserve the tradition of making dugout canoes. A seagoing vessel begins as a single tree trunk.
options.label: legacy.discoverdominica.com

options.text: Dominica's European name records a day of the week. Columbus sighted the island on a Sunday in 1493.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Morne Trois Pitons National Park alone contains five volcanoes. Within one patch of this small Caribbean island are hot springs, freshwater lakes and geothermal vents.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Owia on Saint Vincent, an old lava formation acts as the wall of a swimming pool. Atlantic waves break over the rock and replenish the salt water inside.
options.label: tourism.gov.vc

options.text: Sailing south through one country can take you from Saint Vincent’s black volcanic beaches to pale coral sands in the Grenadines. The grains on either shore come from quite different sources.
options.label: nationalparks.gov.vc

options.text: The Saint Vincent parrot’s whole native range is on the country’s main volcanic island. The neighbouring Grenadines fall outside it despite sharing the same national borders.
options.label: nationalparks.gov.vc

options.text: France is one of Saint Lucia’s closest neighbours. The island across the channel to the north is Martinique, so a short sea crossing takes you from an independent Caribbean country to French territory.
options.label: portal-uat.who.int

options.text: Saint Lucia bears the name of a real woman, Saint Lucy of Syracuse. An island in the Caribbean took the name of a woman from another island, Sicily, on the far side of the Atlantic.
options.label: externalaffairs.govt.lc

options.text: The Saint Lucia parrot’s entire native range lies within one small island, and even there it keeps largely to the forested interior. A flight across the channel to a neighbouring island would take it outside the species’ natural range.
options.label: govt.lc

options.text: At Carnival on Carriacou, rival performers recite Shakespeare in costume. Remembering lines from Julius Caesar belongs to a distinctly Grenadian tradition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wooden boatbuilders on Carriacou and Petite Martinique pass on their eye for a hull's shape through hands-on apprenticeship.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Grenada put one of its crops directly on its flag. The small emblem by the hoist is a nutmeg.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Grenada has an active volcano that never breaks the surface. Kick-'em-Jenny rises from the Caribbean seabed just north of the main island.
options.label: uwiseismic.com

options.text: At the Baths on Virgin Gorda, huge granite boulders lean together over the shore and make passages, pools and grottoes among the rocks.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: Anegada is flat and made of coral limestone. It has a very different silhouette from the other main islands of the British Virgin Islands.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: The RMS Rhone sank off Salt Island in a hurricane in 1867. Its wreck has become one of the territory's best-known dive sites.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: Anegada's great offshore barrier, Horseshoe Reef, is far more extensive than the low island it protects. Ships could hit the reef before the island itself was easy to see.
options.label: bvitourism.com

options.text: On Salt Cay, workers used gates and wind-powered pumps to move seawater from pond to pond. Evaporation left crystals to rake for export.
options.label: www.visittci.com

options.text: The red top of the native Turk's cap cactus resembles a fez. The plant gave the Turks Islands their name and appears on their coat of arms.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: These islands once belonged administratively to Jamaica. Jamaica's independence in 1962 left Turks and Caicos a separate British colony.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The two halves of Turks and Caicos stand on separate shallow banks. Between them the Turks Island Passage drops into water more than a kilometre deep.
options.label: visittci.com

options.text: The blue iguana is native to just one island, Grand Cayman. The Salina Reserve protects habitat for this large, blue-grey reptile.
options.label: nationaltrust.org.ky

options.text: Cayman Brac takes its name from a Gaelic word for a bluff. A limestone escarpment running down the island makes it easy to see why.
options.label: trade.visitcaymanislands.com

options.text: The name Cayman preserves a word for crocodile. Europeans applied the Caribbean name for the animal to the islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Cayman Islands are small exposed summits along a submarine ridge. Just offshore the sea floor drops towards the Cayman Trough, the deepest part of the Caribbean.
options.label: gov.ky

options.text: Wooden sailing boats race as a national sport in Anguilla. Crowds can follow the contest alongshore as well as watching from the water.
options.label: ivisitanguilla.com

options.text: Anguilla's long, slender outline gave it its name. The word means eel in Spanish.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Anguillans resisted being governed together with Saint Kitts and Nevis. A revolt in the 1960s helped set the island on the road to separate administration.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Far north of Anguilla's main island, tiny Sombrero is surrounded by deep water and has no resident human population. This isolated, flat-topped island is an important seabird nesting site.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Willemstad's Queen Emma Bridge floats on pontoons. It swings aside to let ships into the harbour, then returns so pedestrians can cross.
options.label: www.curacao.com

options.text: Willemstad grew in distinct districts around a deep natural harbour. Its buildings combine Dutch planning with Caribbean colours and materials.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Curaçao was once administered with other Dutch Caribbean islands as part of the Netherlands Antilles. In 2010 it became a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Curaçao lies in the dry southern Caribbean near Venezuela. Its natural landscape includes thorn scrub and tall cacti, despite its position well inside the tropics.
options.label: cbs.cw

options.text: Enslaved Africans built Brimstone Hill Fortress on Saint Kitts. The volcanic hill and its great stone works commanded a wide stretch of Caribbean sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A channel called The Narrows separates Saint Kitts and Nevis. It is only about three kilometres across.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Kitts and Christopher are versions of the same name. The island's formal name, Saint Christopher, refers to the same place as Saint Kitts.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest sovereign country in the Americas by land area. Its two main islands together cover only about 260 square kilometres.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The United States has two places named Point Udall thousands of miles apart. The one on Saint Croix honours Stewart Udall and the one on Guam honours his brother Morris.
options.label: congress.gov

options.text: On Saint John, reef-building corals grow among mangrove roots in Hurricane Hole. Shade from the trees can shelter corals in surprisingly shallow water.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: On Saint Croix, Salt River Bay opens straight into a submarine canyon. The seafloor drops away just beyond a sheltered inlet lined with mangroves.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: At Maho Beach, arriving aircraft cross the shore just before touchdown. The runway of Princess Juliana International Airport begins almost at the sand.
options.label: www.vacationstmaarten.com

options.text: The border between Sint Maarten and French Saint Martin passes right across Simpson Bay Lagoon. Someone sailing across the lagoon can change jurisdictions without going out to sea.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Salt helped draw the Dutch to the island in the seventeenth century. The deposits were valuable enough for rival powers to contest them.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Sint Maarten's only land neighbour is France. This Caribbean island is the one place where the Kingdom of the Netherlands and the French Republic have a land border.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A rock off Martinique was commissioned as a British warship. The Royal Navy treated Diamond Rock as a stationary ship because its position commanded a sea passage.
options.label: rmg.co.uk

options.text: Beach sand changes colour across Martinique. Dark volcanic grains dominate parts of the mountainous north, while pale sands line many southern bays.
options.label: martinique.org

options.text: The Martinique oriole has an unusually small country list. Its entire wild range is on this one French Caribbean island, despite other wooded islands just across the channels.
options.label: martinique.developpement-durable.gouv.fr

options.text: You can walk out of the European Union on Saint Martin. The French side is an EU outermost region, while Dutch Sint Maarten is associated with the EU and lies outside its territory.
options.label: ec.europa.eu

options.text: Saint Martin’s salt ponds can switch from briny water to exposed mud or salt as the weather changes. These shallow basins behind the beaches also provide feeding stops for migrating shorebirds.
options.label: reservenaturelle-saint-martin.com

options.text: Two islands in the same French territory are made of surprisingly different rock. Offshore Tintamarre is a flat slab of ancient coral limestone, while much of neighbouring Saint Martin rises in hills of volcanic origin.
options.label: reservenaturelle-saint-martin.com

options.text: The Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes got its name after the 1912 Novarupta eruption. Water heated beneath the fresh deposits escaped through thousands of steaming vents.
options.label: www.nps.gov

options.text: During the Ice Age, lower seas exposed land between Alaska and Siberia. Much of that former land bridge now lies underneath the Bering and Chukchi seas.
options.label: home.nps.gov

options.text: At Brooks Falls, brown bears wait on the lip of the waterfall while salmon try to jump upstream. The obstacle brings bears and fish to exactly the same spot.
options.label: www.nps.gov

options.text: Alaska reaches farther west and farther east by longitude than any other US state. The Aleutian chain crosses the 180th meridian into eastern longitudes.
options.label: alaska.gov

options.text: You can pick out the Nile in a photograph of Egypt at night. Town lights trace the same narrow ribbon as the green fields in daylight, including a great sideways bend near Luxor.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Egypt’s annual Nile flood once delivered fresh soil to farmers. The Aswan High Dam now catches much of that sediment behind it, hundreds of kilometres upstream from fields that used to receive it.
options.label: thirdworldcentre.org

options.text: At Khartoum the Nile begins under that single name where two rivers of different colours meet. From above, the boundary between their waters can remain visible downstream of the junction.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: On the White Nile system, water leaving Lake Victoria passes through two more great lakes before it reaches South Sudan. The river links Victoria, Kyoga and Albert like beads on a string.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Across South Sudan’s Sudd, the White Nile spreads through such extensive marshes that roughly half the water entering the wetland is lost to evaporation and plants before it gets through.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: At Jebel Aulia in Sudan, water from one Nile waits for the other. Operators can hold back the White Nile while the Blue Nile is in flood, then release water after the flood peak has passed.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: The lake that feeds the Blue Nile once dried out. Sediment cores from Lake Tana record a time near the end of the last ice age when the lake could no longer send a steady overflow towards Egypt.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: The Blue Nile can run brown. Summer rain washes soil from the Ethiopian highlands into the river, giving it a muddy colour that satellites can distinguish where it meets the White Nile.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Water leaves Ethiopia’s largest lake by a single outlet. Just downstream, the Blue Nile drops over the falls called Tis Isat before cutting its way out of the highlands.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Soundings in the lower Congo have found more than 200 metres of water beneath the surface. A reach that looks like an ordinary river from the bank conceals a canyon deep enough to swallow a skyscraper.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: Two fish on opposite banks of the lower Congo can be more isolated than fish many kilometres apart on the same side. Powerful currents divide habitats so effectively that separate species have evolved within one river.
options.label: amnh.org

options.text: The Congo basin collects rain on both sides of the equator. As one half moves out of its rainy season, tributaries in the other can still be rising, helping keep the river full year-round.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: The Niger starts relatively close to the Atlantic, then flows inland towards the Sahara. Only after a great bend through Mali does it head back towards the ocean, reaching it in Nigeria.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: The Niger makes a delta twice. It spreads into lakes and marshes in landlocked Mali, gathers back into one channel, and eventually splits again where it reaches the Atlantic.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: A rainstorm upstream can matter more to Mali’s Inner Niger Delta than rain falling on the delta itself. Forecasters use upstream river levels to predict how high the flood will reach farther north weeks later.
options.label: opidin.org

options.text: Victoria Falls has moved. The Zambezi has successively cut through different cracks in the basalt, leaving a zigzag chain of gorges downstream that marks earlier positions of the waterfall.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In western Zambia, the Zambezi spills across the Barotse Plain for months at a time. The plain temporarily stores floodwater, delaying its journey towards Victoria Falls.
options.label: floodbased.org

options.text: At Victoria Falls, a river more than a kilometre wide drops into a narrow crack. Almost the whole Zambezi then escapes through one gap in the opposite wall.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Diamonds that formed inland reached Namibia’s coast by river. The Orange carried them to the Atlantic, where waves and currents sorted them into beach and offshore deposits.
options.label: gem-a.com

options.text: At Augrabies in South Africa, the Orange funnels over a granite ledge and into a steep gorge. In flood, water thunders down channels that stand dry beside the main waterfall for much of the year.
options.label: sanparks.org

options.text: The Orange ends on an international border. At its mouth, the wetland on one side belongs to Namibia and the wetland on the other to South Africa.
options.label: the-eis.com

options.text: The Limpopo starts where the Crocodile and Marico meet. It first runs north, although its mouth is far to the southeast on Mozambique’s Indian Ocean coast.
options.label: limpopocommission.org

options.text: A traveller following the Limpopo downstream can keep South Africa on one bank while the country across the water changes from Botswana to Zimbabwe.
options.label: limpopocommission.org

options.text: In Mozambique’s 2000 floods, the lower Limpopo spread far beyond its ordinary channel. Satellite images showed a broad sheet of water across the plain where individual river bends had been visible before.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In Yunnan, the upper Yangtze runs alongside two other great rivers, the Mekong and Salween. Mountains keep them apart, and the three ultimately reach the sea thousands of kilometres from one another.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: China’s Three Gorges Dam turned a long stretch of the Yangtze into a staircase with one enormous step. Ships use locks to climb from the lower river to a reservoir that reaches hundreds of kilometres upstream.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: At Shigu the upper Yangtze turns so sharply that it starts heading back north. This bend helps send its water across China towards Shanghai while neighbouring rivers continue south.
options.label: visityunnanchina.com

options.text: In parts of its lower course the Yellow River flows above the surrounding plain. Sediment raises the bed between its embankments, so a breach can send the river downhill onto an entirely new route.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: The Yellow River can build a piece of coast and then abandon it. Satellite images show new land forming at the active mouth while waves eat away the land around a former outlet.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Yellow River owes its colour to material it picks up on the Loess Plateau. Much of that fine soil originally arrived on the plateau by wind before the river carried it out to sea.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Mekong makes a tributary run backwards. During the wet season it pushes water up the Tonle Sap River into a Cambodian lake. When the Mekong falls, the lake empties back into it.
options.label: ffw.mrcmekong.org

options.text: At Khone Falls the Mekong breaks into a maze of channels. Fish migrating upstream can pass through particular channels around the falls, so a seemingly small side passage can matter to fisheries far upriver.
options.label: giz.de

options.text: High in China, the Mekong runs in a gorge parallel to the Yangtze and Salween. A short journey across a mountain ridge can put a raindrop on a different route to a different sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Ganges acquires its name at a visible fork in the Himalayas. Two separately named rivers, the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda, meet at Devprayag and continue downstream as the Ganga.
options.label: nmcg.nic.in

options.text: A tiger can live among trees flooded by sea tides at the mouth of the Ganges. The Sundarbans mangroves grow where sediment from the great Bengal rivers meets salt water from the bay.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Water from the Ganges can reach the Bay of Bengal by two national routes. The main channel enters Bangladesh, while the Bhagirathi–Hooghly branch passes Kolkata in India.
options.label: nmcg.nic.in

options.text: The Indus cuts a deep gorge beside Nanga Parbat, a mountain over eight kilometres high. River water and an eight-thousand-metre summit pass remarkably close to each other horizontally.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: Pakistan grows irrigated crops far from the banks of the Indus. A connected network of barrages and canals spreads the river system’s water across one of the world’s largest irrigated areas.
options.label: documents1.worldbank.org

options.text: The Indus starts on the Tibetan Plateau and crosses high, dry Ladakh before reaching Pakistan. Part of the water that ends in the Arabian Sea begins its journey on the far side of the Himalayas.
options.label: lib.icimod.org

options.text: In Tibet the Brahmaputra flows east as the Yarlung Tsangpo, then hooks around the mountain Namcha Barwa and dives into a deep gorge. In Bangladesh its main channel has yet another name, the Jamuna.
options.label: portals.iucn.org

options.text: Old maps of Bangladesh show the Brahmaputra taking a different route to the sea. Over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries its main flow shifted west, leaving the Old Brahmaputra carrying much less water.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: The Brahmaputra can surround a new island without ever reaching the sea. Its channels split and rejoin around bars of sand and silt, and the next flood can rearrange them.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: On Myanmar’s Irrawaddy, wild dolphins and fishers have learned to signal to one another. The dolphins herd fish towards a cast net and catch fish escaping around its edges.
options.label: programs.wcs.org

options.text: The Irrawaddy leaves pictures of its old bends on the plain. When the river cuts across a loop, a crescent-shaped lake can remain beside the new channel.
options.label: eol.jsc.nasa.gov

options.text: Sediment in the Irrawaddy delta has a mountain provenance. Researchers can use the minerals in grains of sand to trace which upstream rocks contributed material to Myanmar’s coast.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: For roughly 2,500 kilometres, the Amur serves as the border between China and Russia. The same stretch is known in Chinese as Heilong Jiang, the Black Dragon River.
options.label: tandfonline.com

options.text: A forest wetland beside the Amur can help feed microscopic plants in the sea. The river carries dissolved iron from inland soils to the Sea of Okhotsk, where that scarce nutrient supports growth.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: The Argun and Shilka lose their names at a single junction. Their combined water becomes the Amur, which later turns away from the international border and reaches the sea in Russia.
options.label: tile.loc.gov

options.text: The Arctic’s largest river delta belongs to the Lena. At the Laptev Sea its single northbound river fans into a maze of channels and islands across the tundra.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Lena flows towards colder country. In spring its southern reaches can thaw while the lower river is still frozen, allowing water and broken ice to pile up behind a downstream ice jam.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Stone pillars line a stretch of the Lena like a wall of towers. Extreme cycles of freezing and thawing helped split ancient limestone into the narrow columns seen from the river.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Ob’s spring flood can run into winter. Meltwater from southern Siberia arrives while the river farther north is still frozen, flooding the broad lowlands behind the ice.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Ob does not open directly into the Arctic Ocean. Its fresh water first travels through the long, narrow Gulf of Ob, an estuary that cuts hundreds of kilometres into Siberia.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: Through its tributary the Irtysh, the Ob collects water that started in China and crossed Kazakhstan. The main Ob itself stays in Russia before reaching the Arctic.
options.label: eabr.org

options.text: The Irtysh runs through a lake on its way from China to Russia. It enters Kazakhstan as the Black Irtysh, passes through Lake Zaysan, and emerges on the other side before eventually joining the Ob.
options.label: eabr.org

options.text: Some Irtysh water travels uphill. The Irtysh–Karaganda canal uses pumping stations to move it away from its natural Arctic-bound route and into the dry interior of Kazakhstan.
options.label: gov.kz

options.text: Follow the Irtysh all the way across three countries and you still have not reached the sea. More than four thousand kilometres from its source, it becomes a tributary of the Ob.
options.label: eabr.org

options.text: The Euphrates has not always drained towards the Persian Gulf. Geologists found evidence that one of its ancient forerunners carried sediment towards the Mediterranean before the drainage network changed.
options.label: nature.com

options.text: Filling a reservoir on the Euphrates changed the geography of a medieval castle. Qalʿat Jaʿbar, once on a hill above the river in Syria, now projects into Lake Assad.
options.label: asor.org

options.text: The Euphrates and Tigris share a final stretch under a different name. After they meet in southern Iraq, their combined channel is called the Shatt al-Arab.
options.label: waterinventory.org

options.text: Iraq can take floodwater out of the Tigris before it reaches Baghdad and send it into Lake Tharthar. The lake occupies a natural hollow between the Tigris and the Euphrates.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Near Baghdad the Tigris comes close to the Euphrates, then bends away again. They run separately across the plain for hundreds more kilometres before finally joining in southern Iraq.
options.label: researchgate.net

options.text: Much of the water the Tigris gains below Mosul comes from its eastern side. The Greater and Lesser Zab drain mountain country towards a main river that is already flowing across the Iraqi plains.
options.label: waterinventory.org

options.text: At the Swiss town of Koblenz, the Aare brings in more water on average than the Rhine arriving from upstream. Below their meeting point, the smaller partner keeps the name.
options.label: dora.lib4ri.ch

options.text: Much of the Rhine reaches the Netherlands and changes its name. The river splits there, and the Waal carries the largest share of its water towards the North Sea.
options.label: undine.bafg.de

options.text: The Rhine flows into and out of Lake Constance. The river that enters the lake from the Alps and the river that leaves it on its way to the Rhine Falls belong to the same watercourse.
options.label: iksr.org

options.text: Europe’s largest river never reaches an ocean. The Volga ends in the Caspian Sea, a closed basin where the water can escape by evaporation.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Europe’s largest river delta spreads along the shore of a lake. Near the Caspian, the Volga breaks into hundreds of channels before its water finally reaches open water.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: One river supplies most of the fresh water entering the Caspian. A change in rainfall far up the Volga can influence the shoreline of a sea shared by five countries.
options.label: hess.copernicus.org

options.text: The sea reaches far inland up the Seine, even where the water tastes fresh. Its tide travels past Rouen and meets its upstream limit at a dam at Poses, about 160 kilometres along the estuary.
options.label: seine-aval.fr

options.text: The lower Seine once had a tidal wave famous enough to draw crowds. The mascaret ran upstream against the river until changes to the channel greatly weakened it.
options.label: seine-aval.fr

options.text: Paris has owned land around the Seine’s springs far outside the city. The river rises on the Langres Plateau in Burgundy, hundreds of kilometres from the capital built on its banks.
options.label: paris.fr

options.text: The Thames once missed London. Gravel left by its ancient channel traces a route farther north, until Ice Age glaciers blocked the way and diverted the river towards its present valley.
options.label: webapps.bgs.ac.uk

options.text: A river still joins the Thames from beneath London’s streets. The Fleet, once an open waterway, was gradually covered over and incorporated into the city’s drains.
options.label: londonmuseum.org.uk

options.text: An unusually high North Sea tide can threaten London from downstream. The Thames Barrier can close across the river to keep that surge out, then reopen as the tide falls.
options.label: gov.uk

options.text: Ships in Hamburg rise and fall with the North Sea even though the port is well inland. The tide runs up the Elbe and changes the water level in the city by several metres.
options.label: tideelbe.info

options.text: The Elbe cuts a canyon through rock once laid down in a sea. The sandstone cliffs continue across the Czech–German border as one landscape, called Bohemian Switzerland on one side and Saxon Switzerland on the other.
options.label: nationalpark-saechsische-schweiz.de

options.text: The Elbe starts as the Labe in Czech mountain country. It reaches the North Sea through Germany, so water from the high ground near Poland can leave Europe west of Denmark.
options.label: northsearegion.eu

options.text: In a dry summer the Adriatic can travel inland up Italy’s longest river. When the Po’s flow weakens, a wedge of denser salt water slips along the bed beneath the fresh water.
options.label: journals.plos.org

options.text: In the early 1600s Venice sent the lower Po down a new route. Diverting its sediment southward helped protect the Venetian lagoon from silting up and set the modern delta growing in a different direction.
options.label: parcodeltapo.org

options.text: The outline of the Po delta records a succession of river mouths. Old ridges of sand now stranded inland mark stretches of former Adriatic beach as the river built new land beyond them.
options.label: iris.cnr.it

options.text: A stretch of the Dnieper once had nine major rapids in succession. Filling the reservoir upstream of the Dnipro dam drowned them, turning a notorious obstacle into navigable water.
options.label: encyclopediaofukraine.com

options.text: After the Kakhovka reservoir drained in 2023, willow seedlings took root on the exposed mud. Part of a lake bed on the lower Dnieper became young woodland within a few growing seasons.
options.label: nauka.gov.ua

options.text: Rivers rising on the Valdai uplands empty into three different bodies of water. The Dnieper heads for the Black Sea, the Western Dvina for the Baltic, and the Volga for the Caspian.
options.label: api.pageplace.de

options.text: The Don and Volga come close in southern Russia, then part for different seas. Their connecting canal lets boats cross the divide between the Sea of Azov and the landlocked Caspian.
options.label: radar.gsa.ac.uk

options.text: An early medieval fortress lies beneath the Don. The site of Sarkel was excavated before the Tsimlyansk reservoir filled and submerged the old riverside settlement.
options.label: hse.ru

options.text: The Don enters a sea shallow enough for its fresh water to transform an entire bay. Water at the eastern end of Taganrog Bay can be nearly fresh, while the Sea of Azov becomes saltier farther west.
options.label: mdpi.com

options.text: Left to itself, more of the lower Mississippi could take a shorter route to the sea through the Atchafalaya. The Old River Control structures keep the flow divided between the two channels.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Mississippi’s active delta looks like a bird’s foot from above. Its narrow fingers are channels carrying sediment so far out into the Gulf that new land follows the branches of the river.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Mississippi has left stripes across its own floodplain. Each time a bend shifted, a ridge or hollow could remain behind, so airborne images reveal a map of channels the river has since abandoned.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The United States’ longest river ends in another river. After crossing the Great Plains, the Missouri gives up its name to the Mississippi near St. Louis, still far from the sea.
options.label: fws.gov

options.text: The Great Falls of the Missouri were five separate waterfalls. For the Lewis and Clark expedition, getting past them meant hauling boats and supplies overland for weeks.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: The Missouri begins among rivers named Jefferson, Madison and Gallatin. Their waters come together near Three Forks in Montana, well east of the Continental Divide.
options.label: dnrc.mt.gov

options.text: The Mississippi’s biggest tributary by volume is the Ohio. The much longer Missouri is a more obvious line on a map, but the Ohio basin generally contributes more water.
options.label: lrd.usace.army.mil

options.text: The Ohio begins at the tip of downtown Pittsburgh. The Allegheny and Monongahela lose their names there, and a third named river starts where the two meet.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: Ice sheets helped assemble the modern Ohio. When glaciers blocked older north-flowing streams, water spilled across divides and carved parts of a new westward route.
options.label: ohiodnr.gov

options.text: Water leaving Columbia Lake in Canada initially travels northwest, away from the US border it will eventually cross. The Columbia loops around a mountain range before turning south.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: Immense Ice Age floods raced down the Columbia Gorge. Water released from glacial Lake Missoula reached the Pacific by forcing its way through the same mountain gap as the Columbia.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: At the Columbia’s mouth, an outgoing river and ebb tide meet incoming Pacific swell. Waves can steepen and break abruptly over the shifting sandbar even when the sea farther out looks manageable.
options.label: stateparks.oregon.gov

options.text: The Mackenzie starts by draining an enormous lake. Water entering Great Slave Lake from the south leaves from its western end and heads north towards the Arctic Ocean.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In the Beaufort Sea, Mackenzie River water can spread as a buoyant layer over denser salt water. Its influence extends well offshore from the river mouth.
options.label: collectionscanada.gc.ca

options.text: Spring can travel down the Mackenzie as a moving front. Open water and broken ice advance from the warmer upstream reaches towards a delta that may still be frozen.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: A Chinook salmon entering the Yukon from the Bering Sea can swim more than 3,000 kilometres inland to spawn. Some finish in Canadian streams close to the mountains above the Pacific coast.
options.label: publications.gc.ca

options.text: Two great Alaskan rivers share the name of a delta without joining each other. The Yukon and Kuskokwim reach the Bering Sea separately across the same broad coastal lowland.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Yukon can flood a town even before all the river ice has melted. Ice breaking upstream can lodge at a bend and briefly dam the river, raising the water behind it.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: Water leaving Lake Ontario enters the St. Lawrence as fresh water, yet farther downstream the same river has tides and beluga whales. The transition to ocean conditions takes place over a long stretch of estuary.
options.label: planstlaurent.qc.ca

options.text: An ocean-going ship can use the St. Lawrence to climb into the Great Lakes. Locks between Montreal and Lake Ontario lift ships past the drop that once made the river’s rapids a barrier.
options.label: greatlakes-seaway.com

options.text: At the mouth of the Saguenay, deep salt water in the St. Lawrence is forced upwards over a rise in the seabed. The food concentrated there helps draw whales to a river junction.
options.label: parcmarin.qc.ca

options.text: When the Rio Grande moved at El Paso, the US–Mexico border became a question about how quickly a river can change. The Chamizal dispute ended in a treaty and a newly engineered channel.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: Much of the water flowing through Big Bend comes from Mexico’s Río Conchos. The Rio Grande can reach their junction with remarkably little water left from its Rocky Mountain headwaters.
options.label: nps.gov

options.text: The same river has different names on opposite banks of the international border. It is the Rio Grande in the United States and the Río Bravo del Norte in Mexico.
options.label: fws.gov

options.text: The Colorado has sometimes turned north near the end of its journey. Sediment on its delta could divert water into the below-sea-level Salton basin, filling a lake instead of sending the flow to the Gulf of California.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: The Colorado carved the Grand Canyon, yet its last stretch can be dry. So much water is withdrawn upstream that its old delta in Mexico often receives little or no river flow.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In 2014 a deliberately released pulse of water travelled down the Colorado’s normally dry channel in Mexico. Water soaked into the sand on the way, briefly bringing stretches of the old river corridor back to life.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: At Manaus, the dark Rio Negro and sandy-coloured Solimões run side by side for kilometres. Their differences in speed, temperature and sediment keep a visible seam in the Amazon downstream of the meeting.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: You can leave the mouth of the Amazon and still be sailing in its water far out at sea. A plume of relatively fresh river water spreads over the saltier Atlantic surface.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: Much of the mud the Amazon delivers to the Atlantic comes from the Andes. Grains eroded from mountains near the Pacific cross almost the full width of South America on the way to the opposite ocean.
options.label: pnas.org

options.text: Where the Paraguay and Paraná meet, their waters can stay visibly separate. Satellite photographs show two colours travelling down one channel near the Argentine city of Corrientes.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Building the Itaipú reservoir drowned the great Sete Quedas waterfalls on the Paraná. The falls had separated fish populations, so their disappearance also redrew an underwater boundary.
options.label: scielo.br

options.text: The Paraná delta is growing towards Buenos Aires. Its many branches drop sediment as they enter the broad Río de la Plata, extending islands at the front of the delta.
options.label: cauceecologico.org

options.text: The Orinoco has a natural exit into the Amazon basin. Part of its flow peels off through the Casiquiare and reaches the Rio Negro, while the rest continues towards the Orinoco’s own delta.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: At Ciudad Guayana, the Caroní sends a dark tongue of water into the muddier Orinoco. From space, it is possible to tell which tributary supplied the water even after it entered the main river.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Atlantic tide reaches into forests at the Orinoco’s mouth. The delta’s branching channels carry water through a landscape that feels both the river’s floods and the rhythm of the sea.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: The Madeira carries an outsized share of the Amazon’s mud. Its headwaters erode the Andes in Peru and Bolivia, sending fine sediment into a much flatter part of Brazil.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: A catfish in the Madeira basin can begin life in the Andean foothills, drift towards the Amazon estuary and later swim back upstream. Dams on the Madeira have interrupted that journey between opposite ends of the basin.
options.label: sinia.minam.gob.pe

options.text: Madeira means wood in Portuguese. During high flows the river undercuts its banks and carries whole tree trunks downstream, giving the river a name you can see floating on its surface.
options.label: philip.inpa.gov.br

options.text: Along most of the border between New South Wales and Victoria, the boundary follows the Murray’s southern bank. A boat out in midstream is on the New South Wales side.
options.label: land.vic.gov.au

options.text: Even Australia’s longest river can struggle to keep its mouth open. Sand builds up where the Murray reaches the sea, and dredges have been used to maintain the opening when river flows are low.
options.label: data.environment.sa.gov.au

options.text: The Murray passes through a lake before it reaches the ocean. Barrages near Lake Alexandrina separate fresh water in the Lower Lakes from saltier water towards the Coorong and the sea.
options.label: environment.sa.gov.au

options.text: The Darling begins when two already substantial rivers meet. Water from the Barwon and Culgoa takes the name Darling downstream of their junction and eventually reaches the Murray at Wentworth.
options.label: parliament.vic.gov.au

options.text: In a dry spell the lower Darling can break into a chain of waterholes. They become refuges for fish until returning flows reconnect them into a river.
options.label: dcceew.gov.au

options.text: A flood on the Darling can be stored beside the river itself. Near Menindee, channels carry water into a chain of natural lakes, where regulators now control part of the exchange with the river.
options.label: waternsw.com.au
